and Debt Flows as of End-2025 Trends in External Debt, 2015–25
Renewed global inflationary pressures, geopolitical tensions, and decreased fiscal space continued to put substantial pressure on the external debt positions of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) in 2025. LMICs’ external borrowing levels reached a record $9.4 trillion at the end of the year, increasing 5.5 percent from $8.9 trillion in 2024. LMIC external debt has grown about 60 percent over the past decade, and the 2025 increase was the largest since the easing of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. The change in debt stock was driven by net debt inflows of $423.5 billion, a more than twofold increase from 2024, as well as by some debt forgiveness and the upward accounting effect of US dollar depreciation.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: During the first half of 2025, the US dollar experienced its biggest depreciation against other currencies in more than five decades, and the increase in new debt flows went largely to middle-income countries (MICs), predominantly because of continued support from multilateral creditors and a rebound in lending from private creditors. That rebound, driven by both new borrowing and buyback operations, indicated a recovery of investor confidence after a retrenchment by private lenders from 2022 to 2023 and only a small increase in 2024, as well as a renewed search for yield (table 1.1). This pattern shows the procyclical nature of the private creditor lending. It expands in favorable global conditions and contracts sharply when conditions tighten.

text: The primary source for these data is reports to the World Bank Group’s Debtor Reporting System (DRS) from member countries that have received either International Bank for Reconstruction and Development loans or International Development Association credits, and that have outstanding obligations to the World Bank Group. The DRS, instituted in 1951, has its origins in the World Bank Group’s need to monitor and assess the financial position of its borrowers. Comprehensive information on data sources and the methodology used to compile the statistics presented in this report can be found in the appendix under “Data Sources.” The following describes the key concepts and data sources.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: • The DRS follows international standards and defines external debt as the outstanding amount of actual current liabilities in both domestic and foreign currency that require payment(s) of principal and/or interest by the debtor at (Box continues on next page)

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text:
some point(s) in the future and that are owed to nonresidents by residents of an economy. The sum of principal and interest payments is defined as debt service.

• The total external debt of a country is the sum of public and publicly guaranteed debt, private nonguaranteed debt, and short-term debt.

• Public and publicly guaranteed external debt comprises long-term external obligations (maturities of over one year) of all public debtors, including debt held by the central government and by state-owned enterprises. Data are collected on a loan-by-loan basis through the DRS. Reporting countries submit quarterly reports on new loan commitments and annual reports on loan status and transactions (new commitments, gross disbursements, principal, and interest payments).

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: • Private nonguaranteed debt comprises long-term external obligations of private debtors that are not guaranteed by a public entity. The DRS has covered private nonguaranteed debt since 1973; however, for this category of debt data, the annual status and transactions (gross disbursements, principal, and interest payments) are reported in aggregate.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: • Short-term debt is defined as debt with an original maturity of one year or less and is not covered under DRS reporting requirements. However, most DRS reporters provide an annual report on outstanding short-term debt stocks on a voluntary basis. For countries that do not provide these data, information on their short-term debt is drawn from the Quarterly External Debt Statistics database, a joint World Bank Group–International Monetary Fund initiative, wherein data are compiled and reported by countries’ central banks, along with data compiled by the Bank for International Settlements.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: All debt data reported to the DRS are validated against—and, when appropriate, supplemented by—data from other sources. These additional data include the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position statistics, Quarterly External Debt Statistics, information published on official government websites, reports from the International Monetary Fund, regional development banks, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the Bank for International Settlements, and websites and annual publications of lending agencies.

The return of debt accumulation to 2019–20 levels indicates both continued support from multilateral creditors and a significant rebound of private investor confidence and lending, as well as LMICs’ eagerness to take advantage of times when international investors are willing to lend.

text: In addition, the short-term debt stock of LMICs increased 4.0 percent to $2.4 trillion at end-2025. These obligations, which are composed of liabilities with a maturity of one year or less and interest arrears on long term debt, stood for 25.7 percent of total external debt, a share that has remained stable over the past decade for LMICs.

The rise was striking because China, which accounts for nearly one-quarter of LMIC debt, continued to reduce its borrowing. These five countries accounted for 29.6 percent of MIC total debt stock. Some of these countries also turned to complex liability management operations to transform the profile of their debt portfolios, as well as total return swap operations, which have gained prominence for LMICs (refer to box 1.2 for definitions and country-specific use of total return swaps).

Box 1.2 Total Return Swaps: An Emerging Form of Sovereign Financing
Total return swaps (TRSs) have traditionally been used in financial markets to transfer the economic risks and returns of an underlying asset without transferring its legal ownership. More recently, TRS structures have gained prominence as a form of sovereign financing, often involving up-front funding and the pledging of government securities or other assets as collateral.

How a TRS Works
A TRS is a financial derivative contract in which one party transfers the total economic return of a reference asset, including income and changes in market value, to another party in exchange for a predetermined stream of payments, typically linked to a benchmark interest rate plus a spread.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text:
In sovereign transactions, TRS structures can combine derivative features with financing. This combination can blur the distinction between a financial derivative and conventional borrowing, and makes it important to assess the economic substance of the transaction.

Sovereign borrowers may turn to TRS arrangements when conventional market financing is unavailable, slow, or prohibitively expensive. By using government (Box continues on next page)

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: securities as collateral, borrowers can obtain foreign currency liquidity quickly and potentially at a lower short-term financing rate. These benefits, however, come with substantial collateral requirements, margin-call, refinancing, and transparency risks.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text:
The Growing Use of TRSs in Sovereign Financing
Since 2024, TRS arrangements have been identified in Angola, Argentina, Colombia, Nigeria, and Senegal, with financing amounts ranging from about $1 .0 billion to $9.3 billion. Maturities have generally ranged from one to three years, and disclosed collateralization ratios have typically been between 133 and 198 percent. Collateral has included domestic government securities, external sovereign bonds, US Treasury securities, or combinations of these instruments. The transactions vary considerably in scale and collateral structure. In Argentina, the central bank entered a $3 billion, three-year TRS in 2025 backed by domestic government securities, although the collateralization ratio has not been publicly disclosed.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Angola entered a $1 .2 billion, one-year transaction in 2024 collateralized at 198 percent, equivalent to about $2.4 billion in collateral, primarily external sovereign bonds. In 2025, this financing was extended and increased to $1 .5 billion for three years, with collateralization reduced to 148 percent, or approximately $2.2 billion. Angola also entered a separate $1 billion, three-year transaction in 2025 collateralized at 140 percent, using a combination of US Treasuries and domestic government securities.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Larger transactions demonstrate the potential scale of this financing. In Colombia, TRS transactions totaling approximately $9.3 billion in 2025 had a one-year maturity and collateralization of about 160 percent, implying approximately $15.1 billion in pledged external and domestic government securities. Nigeria’s $5 billion transaction in 2026 has a three-year maturity and collateralization of approximately 133 percent, corresponding to about $6.7 billion in domestic securities. In Senegal, seven TRS transactions contracted in 2025 provided approximately $1 .1 billion in financing with three-year maturities and average collateralization of about 135 percent, corresponding to approximately $1 .5 billion in pledged domestic government securities.

• Large financing amounts: Transactions range from about $1 .0 billion to $9.3 billion.

text:
Implications for Debt Statistics and Transparency
A TRS is normally a financial derivative, but some structures can also create debt. If the sovereign receives cash up front and is required to repay it regardless of the performance of the underlying assets, the financing creates an unconditional repayment obligation and is therefore recorded as debt. The derivative component is recorded separately. Securities pledged as collateral generally remain on the sovereign’s balance sheet and do not create additional debt simply because they are pledged. The growing use of TRS financing also raises broader transparency and risk-management issues. Headline debt statistics may not fully reveal the amount of collateral pledged, exposure to margin calls, or refinancing and liquidity risks.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Transparent reporting should therefore provide information on the amount financed, maturity, collateralization ratio and type of collateral, margin requirements, repayment obligations, and rollover or early termination provisions, while separately identifying the financing and derivative components. text: External debt, which is usually contracted and denominated in foreign currency, is exposed to year-on-year and intrayear exchange rate fluctuations that affect its rate of accumulation and its debt service payments. Movements in the value of the US dollar against other global currencies affect the value of LMICs’ debt, and the size of these fluctuations in 2025 had important implications for LMICs, particularly those with large dollar-denominated external debt portfolios. For this subset of countries following a flexible exchange rate regime, dollar-denominated debt became cheaper to service.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Additionally, in this publication, the US dollar is used as the common currency by convention to measure all external borrowing of LMICs, which has implications over time. As the US dollar depreciated in 2025 against the euro, the British pound, the Chinese yuan, and many other currencies, the debt stock denominated in those currencies increased when converted to US dollars. The euro, IMF special drawing rights (SDR),2 the Chinese yuan, and the Japanese yen are the four currencies that make up the largest portion of LMICs’ non-dollar-denominated debt. In 2025 the dollar depreciated 13.1 percent against the euro, 5.0 percent against SDR, and 4.4 percent against the yuan, and remained essentially stable against the weakened

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Japanese yen. The dollar’s dramatic 2025 depreciation inflates the size of external debt denominated in these currencies; that debt would appear to be more moderate if, for example, it was recorded in euros or other hard currencies.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: The effect is particularly pronounced among the concessional arm of all multilateral creditors. SDR-denominated loans represent a significant share of outstanding concessional debt across multilateral institutions, and the dollar’s 5.0 percent depreciation against the SDR in 2025 increased these loans’ dollar-equivalent values correspondingly. Concessional repayment schedules further amplify the impact: because annual principal payments are small relative to outstanding balances, the dollar-equivalent currency revaluation of the debt stock tends to outweigh the modest stock reductions from debt servicing.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: For several of the largest borrowers from concessional windows, currency valuation gains in 2025 not only offset principal payments made during the year but also, in some cases, partially reversed the stock reductions achieved through repayments in 2024, leaving reported balances higher at end-2025 despite continued debt servicing. Of the $301.8 billion increase in LMICs’ PPG debt stock (external debt obligations of a country’s government and any private sector debts backed by a public sector guarantee) recorded in 2025, at least 28.2 percent can be attributed to the depreciation of the US dollar. Borrowing by the PPG sector of the economy gets reported at the instrument level and in the currency in which the liabilities are denominated or repaid.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Accordingly, this level of detailed reporting makes possible the computation of the effect of the cross-currency valuation. Viewed from a lending category perspective, the external debt stock of countries eligible for International Development Association (IDA) financing increased 8.1 percent in 2025, to $1.3 trillion. Of this group, LICs’ debt increased at an even faster pace of 8.9 percent in 2025, to $262.4 billion, a marked increase not seen since 2020. Although LICs account for only a 2.8 percent share of total LMIC debt stock, over 60 percent of these countries are at high risk of debt distress or already in debt distress.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: An increase of such magnitude for this most vulnerable group of countries exacerbates their susceptibility to financial market volatility and stresses their already limited fiscal space. (Refer to box 1.3 for income and lending classifications.)

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Private lending, which is more susceptible to fluctuations in financial market conditions, pricing conditions, and perceived creditworthiness of the borrower, saw a strong rebound in 2025. LMIC debt stock owed to private creditors increased 5.2 percent in 2025 to $5.0 trillion, compared to the 0.6 percent increase recorded in 2024. The increase in debt stock owed to private creditors was due to a combined increase in debt owed to bondholders and to commercial banks and other private creditors, which increased by 5.7 percent (to $2.4 trillion) and 4.7 percent (to $2.7 trillion), respectively (figure 1.2).

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Almost three-fourths of total LMIC debt stock owed to bondholders was issued by public sector entities; that share increased 6.2 percent in 2025, to $1.8 trillion. The increase is even more pronounced when China is excluded: debt stock owed to bondholders increased 11.1 percent, to $1.8 trillion, and debt stock owed to commercial banks and other private creditors rose 8.3 percent, to $2.3 trillion (figure 1.3). The increase in private lending, which is highly procyclical, was correlated with this group of countries’ robust economic growth, as measured by their gross national income (GNI), which grew 6.0 percent in 2025.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Through the most recent crises, decreases in debt stock from this creditor base have been associated with the 2008 financial crisis, the 2015 turbulence, and the COVID-19 pandemic. The robust 2025 economic growth of LMICs (excluding China) attracted lenders back to these economies, and many LMIC governments proved eager to borrow when international investors are willing to lend, even at elevated borrowing rates. For this group of countries, the share of debt stock owed to bondholders by public sector entities stands at 82 percent, a much higher share than the PNG sector counterpart, and increased by 10.4 percent to $1.5 trillion in 2025.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text:
The opposite is true for debt stock owed to commercial banks and other private creditors, where an 83 percent share of the obligations is held by the PNG sector of the economy. This type of debt increased 7.0 percent to $1.9 trillion in 2025, and the debt stock of public sector entities owed to commercial banks and other private creditors saw a much larger increase of 15.1 percent, to $385.7 billion in 2025.

(Box 1.4 describes the international support for Ukraine through this initiative.) LMICs’ debt stock owed to multilateral creditors increased 9.6 percent to $1.5 trillion in 2025. text: Box 1.4 International Support for Ukraine: The G-7 Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration A Surge in Lending, Concentrated Among Official Creditors Financial support for Ukraine from bilateral and multilateral creditors has reached unprecedented levels since the start of the Ukraine War in February 2022. Official creditors, including the Group of Seven (G-7) bilateral creditors and multilaterals like the European Union and the World Bank Group, provided $122.2 billion in disbursements during the 2022–25 period. This support reshaped the composition of Ukraine’s external debt (figure B1 .4.1).

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Long-term external debt stock rose from $99 billion in 2015 to $227 billion in 2025, but little of that increase was driven by private creditors, whose claims remained broadly flat over the past decade, rising slightly from $72 billion to $82 billion. Debt owed to multilateral creditors accounts for most of the increase. Bilateral claims increased sixfold over the past decade but grew from a much smaller base and remained a modest share of the total. These official creditors delivered support to Ukraine not only through direct lending but also through grants, trust funds, guarantees, and co- and parallel financing, among other financial instruments.

The ERA and the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism
One such distinct lending mechanism is the G-7 Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) Loans to Ukraine initiative, agreed in October 2024. Under the ERA, G-7 members committed approximately $50 billion in support to Ukraine. (Box continues on next page)

(Box continues on next page)

What is unique about this mechanism, compared to direct lending, is that the principal and interest are serviced from future revenues generated by immobilized Russian sovereign assets rather than from Ukraine’s own budget. Those revenues are channeled through the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism, administered by the European Commission. ERA support extended as loans creates a repayment obligation for the government of Ukraine and is therefore recorded as an external debt liability, whereas the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism represents a financial asset of Ukraine available to service the loan.

Accordingly, borrowing remains a debt liability even when debt service is expected to be financed from proceeds of immobilized or seized assets. Those proceeds provide the mechanism for repayment but do not change the nature of the liability.

Trends in External Debt Flows, 2015–25
Net debt inflows (disbursements minus principal repayments) to LMICs grew for a third consecutive year, more than doubling in 2025 to $423.5 billion. From a maturity standpoint, short-term net debt inflows recorded a more than fivefold increase in 2025, to $89.4 billion, and long-term net debt inflows doubled, to $334.1 billion, approximately 78.9 percent of the total volume of net inflows. This increase in long-term net debt inflows was due to the return to lending to LMICs by private creditors in 2025; these creditors accounted for 75.2 percent of the total long-term component and increased their lending volume by 180.5 percent to $251.1 billion.

The increase in new public sector disbursements was driven by Mexico, which accounted for a 16.7 percent share of new LMIC issues, at $42.0 billion in 2025. Türkiye and Colombia were the next largest LMIC public sector issuers, at $27.7 billion and $27.5 billion respectively, which reflects strong international investor demand in 2025.

text: The headline issuance figure masks a divergence of the use of the proceeds from these international bond sales, however. Some of the proceeds from new debt issuances in 2025 were strategically used to fund LMICs’ ongoing and proactive liability management strategies and operations, particularly debt buyback operations. Fourteen countries carried out such operations to prepay and mature $34.5 billion of their outstanding external debt obligations.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: The debt management strategies included the use of proceeds from the issuance of new bonds to mature existing liabilities and were part of larger operations, in efforts to alter the maturity structure of these countries’ debt portfolios, to change the currency in which the debt is denominated in order to reduce exchange rate exposure, or to lower the interest rates being charged. Bullet payments of bond obligations coming due over the 2024–26 redemption wall were pushed further into the future through these operations, easing rollover risk pressures.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: In June and September of 2025, Mexico’s public sector executed several debt management operations, including issuing new international bonds to retire existing sovereign and state-owned enterprises’ liabilities for an equal or lesser nominal value. These buyback operations totaled $17.6 billion and aimed to extend the maturity profiles of existing liabilities and to lower borrowing costs by capturing lower interest rates. Other markets also recorded major buyback operations, with Colombia at $6.6 billion and Argentina at $2.8 billion, recording the second- and third-largest LMIC operations. Both countries used debt buyback operations in 2025 to retire existing bonds before maturity, with

text: the goal of lengthening the maturity profiles of their portfolios and reducing the cost of servicing these obligations. In 2025, Kenya issued new bonds of $3.5 billion that were used to execute two debt buyback operations, the largest from an IDA-eligible country, at $1.2 billion. The proceeds were used to smooth the maturity profile of existing liabilities by refinancing near-term liabilities with longer-dated debt, including the $900 million Eurobond maturing in 2027 and the $1 billion Eurobond maturing in 2028. Net debt inflows from official multilateral creditors accounted for 89.4 percent of the official flows, increasing 3.8 percent to $74.1 billion in 2025. Net debt flows from the World Bank Group (International Bank for
Reconstruction and Development [IBRD] and IDA financing) continued to remain positive in 2025, at $20.0 billion. Unlike procyclical lending from private creditors, lending from official creditors, including multilateral institutions, is highly countercyclical in nature. During the COVID-19 pandemic and its aftermath, the World Bank Group and other multilateral institutions stepped up their financing to stabilize LMIC economies through budget support lending, especially for the most vulnerable IDA-eligible countries, as private creditors and

text: market financing retrenched. text:
Trends in Net Transfers on External Debt, 2015–25
LMICs’ long-term net debt transfers (disbursement minus total debt service payments) turned positive in 2025 after three consecutive years of negative volumes. Negative net transfers were recorded since 2022, during the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, indicating that LMICs’ new disbursements were lower than what they paid in interest and principal payments to service their debt obligations. In 2025, net debt transfers on long-term debt turned positive, reversing from an outflow of $118.4 billion in 2024 to an inflow of $45.4 billion (figure 1.7). The improvement was due to net transfers to PPG borrowers, which increased more than sevenfold to $49.9 billion, after turning slightly positive in 2024 to $6.6 billion.

Net transfers to PNG borrowers remained negative for the fourth consecutive year but improved considerably, from an outflow of $125.0 billion in 2024 to an outflow of $4.5 billion in 2025. The substantial rise in new gross financing of 17.3 percent, combined with a much slower increase of 2.3 percent in debt service payments, resulted in the improvement in long-term net transfers to LMICs in 2025. This change is even more pronounced when China is excluded. Net transfers on long-term debt to LMICs excluding China reversed from an outflow of $48.5 billion to an inflow of $200.5 billion.

LMICs’ average interest rate on new external commitments from private creditors remained elevated in 2025, at 5.7 percent, almost double the rate of the equivalent from official creditor sources (figure 1.9). Average interest rates began to increase rapidly in 2022 to tame inflation and have remained elevated since then for private creditors, whose lending tends to oscillate depending on market conditions. Following the effective closure of the market to high-yield issuers during 2022–23, primary market activity has rebounded decisively.

text: Box 1.5 Early 2026 Data Show No Signs of Slowdown in LMIC Bond Market Activity Preliminary data on public and publicly guaranteed (PPG) bond issuances for the first seven and a half months of 2026 show no signs of a slowdown in the appetite of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) for external capital market financing. In fact, more than 10 countries had already surpassed their full-year 2025 PPG bond totals before 2026 reached its midpoint, and the share of bond issuances with maturities of 10 years or more rose as well.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: The breadth of market access expanded notably in the first months of 2026. Several countries accessed international bond markets as PPG issuers without having done so at all in 2025. For example, the Democratic Republic of Congo issued $1 .25 billion across two bonds at coupons of 8.75 and 9.50 percent, among the highest sovereign coupon rates recorded in 2026 so far.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: For several countries, issuance volumes through mid-August 2026 already exceeded their full-year 2025 totals. Angola issued $4.75 billion through mid- August 2026, more than double the $2.01 billion issued across all of 2025. Its weighted average coupon also rose to 9.6 percent, up from 8.6 percent in 2025. Bosnia and Herzegovina raised $1 .8 billion through mid-August, versus $412 million for all of 2025. India more than doubled its full-year 2025 PPG bond total of $1 .0 billion by mid-August 2026, raising $2.5 billion. Indonesia and the Philippines also surpassed their respective 2025 full-year totals.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Borrowing costs for the most vulnerable economies remained elevated and, in several cases, rose further. For Sub-Saharan African issuers specifically, the weighted average coupon on PPG bonds rose from 8.0 percent in 2025 to 8.8 percent through mid-August 2026, and the average maturity on new Sub- Saharan African PPG bonds shortened from 10.4 years in 2025 to 8.9 years, a simultaneous deterioration in both the cost and the tenor of market access. Across the broader LMIC universe, maturities lengthened compared with 2025, reflecting a shift toward longer-tenor issuances among major borrowers. Bonds with maturities of 10 years or more accounted for 41 .5 percent of total PPG issuance volume through mid-August 2026, up from 36.1 percent across all of 2025.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Several major issuers, including Brazil, Mexico, and Türkiye, issued across multiple maturity tranches in a single transaction, a structure that allows borrowers to simultaneously refinance near-term obligations and extend their debt profiles. This maturity extension has unfolded against a backdrop of elevated global borrowing costs. Through mid-2026, benchmark government bond yields in major advanced economies reached multiyear highs, reflecting persistent inflationary pressures, rising public debt issuance volumes across advanced economies, and a prolonged period of restrictive monetary policy. Trends in Equity and Personal Remittances Flows, 2000–25
External debt flows should be considered alongside other cross-border financing flows that shape the resources available to LMICs. These financing flows include equity flows—foreign direct investment (FDI) and portfolio equity (PE)—as well as personal remittances. Together, they provide a broader view of the changing composition of external finance and the different forms of external resources available to LMICs. Aggregate financial inflows, comprising debt and equity flows, provide an important measure of cross-border financial integration.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025
metadata.section: Trends in Equity and Personal Remittances Flows, 2000–25

text: Within the equity component, FDI captures investment associated with a lasting interest in an enterprise and PE captures nonresident purchases and sales of equity securities classified as portfolio investment. Personal remittances are considered separately because they are transfers rather than financial account flows, but they issuances are priced at a spread above these advanced economy benchmarks, meaning that structurally higher reference rates feed through directly into the total cost of new market borrowing.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025
metadata.section: Trends in Equity and Personal Remittances Flows, 2000–25

text: In this environment, 2026 has seen another year of large-scale liability management operations, with new issuance used to buy back existing bonds maturing in the near term, a pattern that helps smooth redemption profiles but does not significantly reduce the underlying stock of debt. Countries entering this environment with elevated debt stocks, limited fiscal space, and near-term maturities face the prospect of having to refinance obligations originally contracted at significantly lower rates, adding to already-strained debt service burdens.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025
metadata.section: Trends in Equity and Personal Remittances Flows, 2000–25

text: Taken together, early 2026 PPG bond data suggest that LMIC governments have maintained robust access to international capital markets, even as the cost of that access, particularly for lower-income and frontier borrowers, has climbed. The expansion in the number of countries issuing, the pace of issuance relative to 2025, and maturities for select countries all point to continued, if increasingly expensive, engagement with private creditors. For Sub-Saharan African issuers, the combination of higher coupons and shorter maturities signals a particularly adverse shift in financing conditions that compounds already-constrained fiscal positions.

text:
Key Debt Indicators, 2015–25
In 2025, LMICs’ external debt ratios remained mainly stable from the peak levels recorded during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020; however, aggregate improvement was uneven, with debt stock ratios rising or holding flat while debt service and interest payment ratios declined across most borrower groups. This change in ratios reflects a combination of strong export and income growth, the completion of debt restructuring agreements in several IDA-eligible countries, and the depreciation of the US dollar, which inflated the dollar-measured value of both debt stocks and GNI simultaneously through an accounting effect, partly moderating ratio movements in both directions.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Ratios of debt to national income and exports are valuable indicators of countries’ ability to service their debt. For LMICs excluding China, the external debt-to-GNI ratio increased from 33.5 percent in 2024 to 34.5 percent in 2025, as the rise in debt stock of 9.1 percent exceeded GNI growth of 6.0 percent in 2025. The external debt stock of the group reached $7.2 trillion in 2025, an increase of 56.4 percent compared to 2015, reflecting a decade of external borrowing that has increased the debt burden in absolute terms. LMICs excluding China improved in the overall debt service-to-GNI ratio, from 5.1 percent in 2024 to 4.7 percent in 2025, with total debt service declining from $1 trillion to $979 billion.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text:
Moreover, interest payments also declined modestly, with the interest payment-to-GNI ratio declining from 1.5 in 2024 to 1.4 percent in 2025.

The external debt-to-GNI ratio in IDA-eligible countries declined from 42.1 percent in 2024 to 41.2 percent in 2025, an improvement after two consecutive years of increases that took the ratio from 30.5 percent in 2015 to its peak in 2024 (figure 1.16). This improvement was driven by GNI growth of 10.5 percent that outpaced the 8.1 percent increase in debt stock. The debt service-to-GNI and interest-to-GNI ratios for IDA-eligible countries declined from 4.2 percent and 1.4 percent in 2024 to 3.7 percent and 1.3 percent, respectively, in 2025, reflecting a 2.3 percent decrease in total debt service obligations and stable interest payments.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Similarly, LICs recorded a marginal deterioration in their external debt-to-GNI ratio, which rose from 41.1 percent in 2024 to 42.3 percent in 2025, as debt stock growth outpaced income growth; the debt service-to-GNI ratio remained broadly stable at approximately 2.0 percent in both years. The interest-to-GNI ratio also improved slightly, from 1.1 percent in 2024 to 1.0 percent in 2025, supported by income growth outpacing flat interest payments of $6.0 billion. Yet interest costs for this group have grown at nearly double the annual average rate recorded over the 2015–25 period, reflecting the structural rise in borrowing costs in recent years.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: The 2025 data point to a range of outcomes for the group and regions, with a few recording distinct trends. Sub-Saharan Africa continued to carry one of the heaviest debt burdens relative to income, with the debt-to-GNI ratio at 48.0 percent, well above the 34.4 percent recorded in 2015 and equivalent to nearly half of the region’s annual national income. Debt service and interest payments relative to GNI, at 4.4 and 1.6 percent, respectively, remained among the highest recorded for the region over the decade, but both ratios are partly weighted by South Africa’s contribution to the regional aggregate.

metadata.chapter_title: Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025

text: Europe and Central Asia retained the highest debt service-to-GNI and interest-to-GNI ratios among all LMIC regions in 2025, at 7.9 and 2.2 percent respectively; however, the debt service-to-GNI ratio declined slightly from 8.1 percent in 2024, and the interest-to-GNI ratio remained stable. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan region recorded the largest single-year increase in its debt-to-GNI ratio of any region, rising from 26.7 to 29.4 percent, signaling continued stock accumulation even as its debt service ratios improved by 0.4 percentage point in 2025 to 3.1 percent.

Trends in External Debt of IDA-Eligible Countries, 2015–25
External debt stock of IDA-eligible countries reached a record $1.3 trillion in 2025, accumulating at a rate of 8.1 percent, faster than that of the other LMICs. The pace of accumulation was much higher than the 2.9 percent average recorded during the past three years and raises sustainability concerns for this group of countries. Long-term debt stock rose by 7.9 percent, and short-term debt rose by 10.7 percent, bringing the end-2025 external debt stock to almost double the 2015 level. Long-term obligations of the PPG sector grew at a faster rate of 9.0 percent than the 4.3 percent increase of the PNG debt stock.

text: Efforts to enhance the debt restructuring architecture continued in 2025 primarily through reforms to the G-20 Common Framework, facilitated by the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable. Debt Restructuring in 2025
Debt restructuring in 2025 focused on implementation of an MoU between bilateral creditors and Ghana, Sri Lanka, and Zambia. As discussed in detail in International Debt Report 2025, all three countries finalized and concluded a restructuring agreement with bondholders in 2024. Tenders by LMICs to buy back or exchange sovereign bonds increased markedly in 2025 as governments used new bond issuance to refinance existing obligations and actively manage their debt portfolios. Implications External Debt, External Shocks, and Vulnerability in LMICs
Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are facing historically high global uncertainty at a time when external debt stocks have reached historic highs, debt service pressures remain elevated, fiscal space is limited in many countries, and global bond yields continue to rise, tightening financial conditions. This combination matters because external shocks can be more difficult to absorb when governments already face substantial financing needs and limited room to respond. The key vulnerability therefore lies not in exposure to global shocks alone but in how those shocks interact with already-high debt burdens.

metadata.section: External Debt, External Shocks, and Vulnerability in LMICs

text: Adverse developments in trade, commodity markets, growth, exchange rates, and tighter global financing conditions all have the potential to weaken external and fiscal positions, and high debt levels can amplify their economic and development consequences and impair the effectiveness of policy responses.

metadata.section: External Debt, External Shocks, and Vulnerability in LMICs

text: International Debt Report 2025 documented the scale of external debt burdens and their links to economic growth and vulnerability (World Bank 2025). Building on that assessment, this year’s report focuses on the interactions between external shocks and external debt burdens, and how debt might amplify vulnerabilities when global conditions deteriorate. This chapter examines the channels through which these interactions operate across LMICs. The chapter further discusses how rising debt service burdens, elevated financing needs, and changing financing patterns are constraining fiscal space and intensifying debt and rollover risks, as well as the policy priorities for strengthening resilience.

text: Finally, food and nutrition security provides a concrete example of these interactions, illustrating how debt burdens may be closely associated with a decline in the affordability of a healthy diet during periods of global stress. The World Uncertainty Index measures broad uncertainty and rose more than fivefold between the third quarter of 2024 and the third quarter of 2025, nearly twice its COVID-19 peak. The Global Economic Policy Uncertainty Index showed a similar pattern, rising sharply in early 2025 and remaining elevated into 2026 (Ahir et al. 2022; Davis 2016).1

metadata.section: External Debt, External Shocks, and Vulnerability in LMICs

text: Elevated uncertainty matters because economies remain closely connected to international markets. Yet countries differ in the nature and degree of their external exposure, which shapes how global external shocks affect them. Trade provides an important example. As figure 2.2 shows, global imports and exports of goods and services increased from below 25 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the early 2000s, were halted by the 2008 global financial crisis, and subsequently rebounded and have fluctuated around 30 percent. Exposure, however, varies significantly across income groups. In 2025, imports accounted for about 34 percent of GDP in low-income economies, compared with exports of about 24 percent; trade flows were much more balanced in high-income economies.

metadata.section: External Debt, External Shocks, and Vulnerability in LMICs

text: The next section discusses these transmission channels in greater detail, including the roles of trade and financial exposure, exchange rates, inflation, and policy buffers, and how external debt can amplify vulnerabilities when shocks occur.

metadata.section: External Debt, External Shocks, and Vulnerability in LMICs

text:
Transmission of External Shocks
External shocks are transmitted to LMICs differently, depending on their structural features. Economies that rely heavily on imports of goods and services for domestic activity are vulnerable to sudden changes in the external environment, such as production shortfalls in major supplier countries, export restrictions, or supply chain disruptions; in contrast, export-oriented economies are more vulnerable to shifts in demand among their trading partners. External shocks also tend to spill more forcefully into LMICs with open financial markets, partly reflecting rapid capital flow movements. In addition, the types of policy frameworks in LMICs are important for the transmission of external shocks.

For example, in economies with flexible exchange rate regimes, the effects of external shocks are partly absorbed through currency movements. In economies with fixed exchange rate regimes, pressure on the exchange rate can be cushioned by using foreign reserves. As discussed later in this chapter, damage from external shocks that LMICs can absorb and the speed of subsequent recovery are also subject to the availability of fiscal buffers and the implementation of fiscal and foreign exchange policy frameworks.

External debt is a key amplifier of the transmission of external shocks. Economies with elevated external debt levels, especially short-term debt, are vulnerable to sudden shifts in investor risk appetite and rollover risks, potentially leading to sudden stops in capital flows and current account reversals. For most LMICs, where external debt tends to be denominated in foreign currencies, economic vulnerabilities can increase when external shocks lead to currency depreciation, causing an increase in debt service burdens and higher inflation. An increase in debt service costs can slow investment growth by decreasing national savings.

During periods of tightening global financial conditions, LMICs with high levels of external debt need to raise interest rates to defend their currencies, causing credit crunches in domestic financial markets and slowing growth.

Despite a recent slowdown in international integration, LMICs have become more exposed to external shocks, while also accumulating external debt. In LMICs, although the pace of trade integration has slowed, trade openness, measured as the sum of exports and imports as a share of GDP, increased to about 48 percent in 2025, up from about 44 percent in the mid-2010s (figure 2.3).

International financial integration has slowed since the pandemic in 2020, but that slowdown has been driven primarily by major economies; financial openness increased in almost 70 percent of LMICs between 2015–19 and 2020–24. In addition, as presented in chapter 1, external debt stocks in LMICs rose to $9.4 trillion by the end of 2025, an increase of $3.5 trillion since 2015.

The nature of external shocks also affects the different degrees of shock transmission to LMICs. For example, global supply shocks, including shortages of energy, food, and other commodities—and rapid increases in their prices, which tend to be caused by wars and conflicts as well as extreme weather-related events—have a larger impact on commodity importers. The outbreak of a conflict involving major commodity producers can halt their exports, and the impact can be exacerbated by logistical disruptions such as port or shipping lane closures. Particularly in food-producing economies, disasters associated with extreme weather, including storms and droughts potentially caused by El Niño, can decrease global food production and disrupt global trade.

In addition, abrupt shifts in trade policies, including the imposition of tariffs or export bans, can restrict access to key commodities. In contrast, commodity exporters tend to be affected more by adverse global demand shocks, including slowdowns in global activity triggered by major systemic events such as financial crises and pandemic-driven lockdowns, and the resulting plunges in commodity prices.

In commodity-importing LMICs, external shocks can be transmitted
through multiple channels. Higher global energy and food prices, along with disruptions to shipping and global value chains, raise production and transportation costs. The resulting rise in domestic inflation in these economies drives up the cost of living, with disproportionate effects on poorer economies and households, where food accounts for a larger share of consumption. The purchasing power of consumers declines as real incomes fall, resulting in reduced spending. In addition, higher prices of commodities and other imported materials increase overall import costs, worsening terms of trade and current account balances.

Financial conditions can tighten because of hikes in interest rates to combat increased inflation, raising borrowing costs. Pressures of currency depreciation rise, increasing the costs of servicing debt denominated in foreign currencies. Fiscal positions deteriorate, with increasing spending pressures, including fuel and food subsidies, and slower activity can lower revenue collection.

Inflation in commodity-importing LMICs has increased following a major energy supply shock in 2026. The conflict in the Middle East involving major energy producers, which began at the end of February 2026, has caused a surge in headline inflation in these countries, to 3.6 percent in June 2026, from the preconflict level of 2.6 percent (figure 2.4). Among market participants, inflation expectations for 2026 have also risen, from 2.7 percent according to preconflict February surveys to 3.4 percent in July. Excluding China, which has been relatively insulated from the shock, partly because of its large petroleum reserves, inflation in commodity-importing LMICs increased from 7.0 percent to 8.3 percent between January and June, with higher inflation expectations for 2026.

Energy prices have increased, as well, by 1.1 percentage points between January and June 2026 (excluding China). To ease price pressures, several central banks have raised interest rates. In addition, several commodity-importing LMICs have introduced subsidies in response to higher fuel prices (World Bank 2026b).

Currency pressures have made imports more expensive in commodity importers and worsened trade balances. Across commodity-importing LMICs with flexible or adjustable currency regimes, merchandise import values, in US dollar terms, increased by an average 23 percent between February and June 2026 compared with the same months of 2025. Excluding China, the rate of increase was 21 percent, on average. As import values increased faster than those of exports, merchandise trade deficits—without China—expanded in the first half of 2026. Between February and June 2026, merchandise trade deficits averaged almost $20 billion higher than in the same months of the previous year.

Global demand shocks affect commodity-exporting LMICs directly and indirectly. Collapses in global commodity prices directly reduce export earnings and profits in the commodity-related sector, reducing domestic demand and activity. Revenue declines cause deterioration of fiscal positions and the debt service mechanism, while also leading to worsening terms of trade and current account balances. With reduced debt repayment capacity, sovereign risk premiums increase, raising debt refinancing costs, eroding investor confidence, and potentially triggering sudden capital outflows. Financial conditions are tightened, with lower credit availability and a weakened banking sector, along with a rise in nonperforming loans.

Declines in foreign exchange earnings also lead to currency depreciation, which increases inflationary pressure and living costs.

The impact of external shocks tends to be larger and more persistent in fragile economies and low-income countries (LICs). In both LICs and economies in fragile, conflict, and violence-affected environments or with institutional fragility, financial markets tend to be shallower than in other LMICs, making them more exposed to external shocks. They tend to rely on narrower economic bases, in terms of exports and revenue sources, and are therefore more affected by sudden shifts in external conditions. With a weak institutional framework and limited access to financing, these economies tend to implement procyclical fiscal tightening during economic downturns.

Increases in commodity prices and supply shortages translate into substantial losses in economic welfare and income, reflecting persistently low personal savings and acute food insecurity. International reserves and credible monetary policies can help cushion the adverse impact of external shocks in LMICs. The accumulation of foreign exchange reserves can defend against sharp currency depreciation and can be used to pay for imports of commodities and other essential products. LMICs have increased their foreign exchange reserves over the past decade, reaching more than $6 trillion at the end of June 2026. Excluding China, foreign exchange increased to $2.6 trillion in June.

However, the pace of foreign exchange accumulation has slowed since March 2026, particularly in commodity-importing LMICs, mainly because of the conflict in the Middle East (figure 2.6). Facing a rise in import costs driven by currency depreciation, some of these economies have been forced to draw on their reserves. This trend has been exacerbated by outflows of foreign currency, mainly driven by rising global risk aversion. In addition, credible monetary policy frameworks act as critical policy buffers against external shocks in LMICs. They help anchor long-term inflation expectations and reduce the transmission of global shocks, such as commodity price changes and financial market volatility, to domestic inflation.
Preconditions for the effectiveness of the frameworks include greater independence for central banks and transparent communication of monetary policy.

Robust fiscal policy frameworks can also act as strong policy buffers against external shocks. Fiscal rules help manage revenue volatility and excess spending during booms; stabilization funds, especially in commodity-exporting LMICs, can mitigate the procyclicality of fiscal policy by saving revenues during booms and deploying them when commodity prices and revenues collapse. Since 2000, many commodity-exporting LMICs have adopted such frameworks (figure 2.7). However, successful implementation requires strong institutions, including transparency and technical capacity (Vasishtha 2026). Policy priorities differ across LMICs, depending on the strength of institutional capacity and fiscal space.

Economies with weaker capacity need to strengthen tax revenue mobilization and improve fiscal transparency.

Debt Sustainability and Fiscal Pressures
External shocks have compounded preexisting fiscal pressures and increased debt vulnerabilities in LMICs. These countries require substantial investment to raise productivity, create jobs, and advance broader development objectives. Financing these needs depends on mobilizing domestic resources, attracting domestic and foreign private capital, and, where necessary, borrowing through public channels. In this context, part of the increase in public debt reflects efforts to finance infrastructure, human capital, and other investments that can support long-term growth. However, slower global growth, policy uncertainty, trade fragmentation, geopolitical tensions, and commodity-price volatility have affected both the availability and cost of financing.

In many countries, shocks that initially generated temporary financing needs have contributed to persistently higher debt stocks, debt service burdens, and rollover requirements.

The Impact of Higher Debt on Fiscal Space and Financing Pressures
The accumulation of public debt has been accompanied by a substantial increase in debt service burdens in LMICs over the past 25 years. The median total debt service in countries eligible for International Development Association (IDA) assistance increased from about 15 percent of government revenues (excluding grants) in 2000 to over 40 percent in 2025. During the same period,

the composition of IDA countries’ debt burden shifted markedly toward domestic debt; whereas average external debt service underwent a U-shaped trajectory to end up at over 17 percent of revenues by 2025, the average domestic debt service-to-revenues ratio more than trebled, reaching almost 30 percent by 2025 (figure 2.8). The increase in the domestic debt service burden was especially pronounced after 2012, reducing the resources available for public investment and other policy priorities, and increasing the need to refinance maturing obligations. As discussed in box 2.1, proactive and structured engagement with investors and creditors can reduce information asymmetries and help lower the uncertainty of premium embedded in borrowing costs.

These developments have contributed to a sustained increase in gross financing needs (GFNs) in IDA countries. Higher debt service burdens have important implications for fiscal space and refinancing needs. A larger share of government revenues must be allocated to interest payments, leaving fewer resources available for public investment and other policy priorities. GFNs in IDA countries averaged about 6 percent of GDP during 2015–19, before increasing to roughly 10 percent during 2020–22 as pandemic-related primary deficits widened and debt service obligations increased. Subsequent shocks, including the commodity price and inflation surge following the Russian Federation’s invasion of Ukraine, and the sharp global monetary tightening that began in 2022, further contributed to elevated financing needs. GFNs subsequently moderated but remained well above their prepandemic average, at approximately 8.2 percent of GDP in 2024, before rising to 8.7 percent in 2025.

Box 2.1 The World Bank Group’s Sovereign Investor Relations Guidance Note Sovereign credit rating actions remained in flux throughout 2025. For instance, in the first half of 2025, Fitch recorded eight sovereign upgrades against four downgrades among emerging markets—a net positive trend—but revised its sector outlook for Asia-Pacific, Eastern Europe, and Sub-Saharan Africa to “deteriorating” from “neutral,” citing trade uncertainty and tightening fiscal space. Moody’s downgraded Bolivia and Botswana, while upgrading Costa Rica.

This mixed picture illustrates that sovereign creditworthiness is increasingly differentiated and that the gap between countries that gain and lose market confidence is often shaped not only by fundamentals but also by how effectively governments engage with investors and creditors.

Against this backdrop, the World Bank Group has published “Sovereign Investor Relations: A Guide for Debt Managers” (Proite and Y avuz 2026), a practical handbook designed to help debt managers in low- and middle-income countries build and professionalize their investor relations functions. The guide argues that countries must move from passive disclosure to active, structured engagement that reduces information asymmetries to lower the “uncertainty premium” embedded in their borrowing costs. The guidance note covers the full spectrum of sovereign investor relations, from strategy formulation to institutional setup as well as practical tools for implementation.

The guide is scalable and designed for countries at varying stages of market development, from frontier markets taking their first steps in external borrowing to frequent issuers seeking to deepen and diversify their investor bases.

The latest developments in 2026 also reinforce the core message of the guidance note—that is, in a world of differentiated sovereign credit outcomes, proactive investor relations are not a luxury but a strategic necessity. Countries that engage creditors early, communicate policy intent clearly, and manage reputational risk systematically are better positioned to preserve market access, reduce financing costs, and navigate periods of stress.

The persistence of high GFNs, despite narrower primary deficits, underscores the role of accumulated debt and higher debt service costs. Notwithstanding notable fiscal consolidation, with primary deficits in 2023–24 narrowing to approximately half their 2021–22 levels, average GFNs stabilized at about 8 percent of GDP, 2 percentage points above their prepandemic average, before increasing further in 2025. Consistent with this pattern, the distribution of debt-stabilization gaps across countries has changed little over the past 15 years (figure 2.9).

These gaps, denoted as ΔDSPD, are calculated as the difference between the actual primary deficit and the debt-stabilizing primary deficit, indicating the primary deficit or surplus that would keep the debt-to-GDP ratio unchanged, given the country’s existing debt, borrowing costs, and GDP growth.2 This calculation suggests that the continued elevation of GFNs is not primarily the result of a renewed widening of primary deficits. Rather, it reflects the debt stock accumulated following successive shocks, higher interest costs, the rollover of maturing obligations, and, in some cases, balance of payments financing needs.

Debt distress risks have eased from the deterioration observed over the past decade, particularly following the COVID-19 shock, but they remain elevated. As informed by the World Bank–International Monetary Fund Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries (LIC-DSF), the number of IDA LIC-DSF countries with unsustainable external public debt or rated as being in debt distress remains limited (at end-December 2025): out of 68 IDA LIC-DSF countries, only 11 are in debt distress or have unsustainable public debt. The share of IDA LIC-DSF countries assessed as being at high risk of external debt distress declined from a peak of 46 percent in 2021 to 35 percent in 2025.
Most emerging markets remain at low or moderate risk of overall sovereign stress,3 although vulnerabilities remain uneven, and debt levels are generally above prepandemic levels.

Despite these improvements, IDA LIC-DSF countries have generally moved from high to moderate risk rather than returning to their preshock levels. Between 2019 and 2025, there were a total of 37 changes in external risk (figure 2.10). Of these changes, 22 were downgraded to higher risk of external debt distress, most of which took place after the COVID-19 shock. More recently, upgrades have reflected improved macro-fiscal conditions and, in a few cases, the completion of debt restructuring. The LIC-DSF framework underpinning these assessments has undergone a comprehensive review by the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund, with that review approved by their respective Executive Boards in September 2026.

The revised framework is expected to be finalized in 2027; box 2.2 summarizes its key features. The revisions aim to strengthen early warning capacity and policy relevance while preserving the framework’s role in guiding borrowing and lending decisions. Key reforms include the following:

• The introduction of new models for the risk of overall public debt stress and public debt unsustainability, together with an updated model for the risk of external public debt stress

The Impact of Debt Composition on Liquidity and Domestic Financial Sector Risks
The increase in financing needs has been accompanied by greater reliance on domestic debt. Domestic borrowing has provided an important source of financing when access to external markets is limited or costly. However, it has also increased rollover risks and strengthened the links between sovereign finances and domestic financial sector stability.

Domestic creditors in both IDA and International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) countries have elevated their exposure to the sovereign over the past 20 years. This move mirrors their respective governments’ growing reliance on domestic financing. However, domestic banks in IDA countries have consistently held a greater share of their balance sheets in sovereign assets than banks in IBRD countries have (figure 2.11). This higher exposure reflects less developed and less diversified private sectors in many IDA countries, as well as fewer investment options as compared to IBRD markets. Domestic banks may therefore have few alternatives to government securities, particularly during periods of financial stress.

In IDA countries, the increase in sovereign exposure goes beyond the domestic banking sector to include the central bank and the domestic nonbanking sector (figure 2.12).

Consequently, domestic debt amortization dominates GFNs for LICs, signaling mounting liquidity pressures even where sovereign solvency appears contained. These pressures reflect the short average maturity of domestic debt in most LICs and the attendant rollover burden, whereby a growing share of gross financing serves merely to refinance maturing domestic obligations. These developments point to intensifying liquidity pressures even where solvency indicators may appear contained, reinforcing the case for monitoring rollover and liquidity risks alongside conventional debt stock metrics.

Fiscal Policy and Debt Management
Higher debt and borrowing costs are absorbing fiscal resources, increasing refinancing risks, and potentially crowding out investment. Weak debt management, limited transparency, foreign currency exposure, and contingent liabilities can amplify these pressures. The result is a reinforcing financing constraint: higher debt service costs reduce fiscal space and limit productive public investment; insufficient public investment weakens the conditions for attracting long-term private capital; and greater reliance on foreign currency

borrowing increases exposure to exchange rate and refinancing shocks. At the same time, high debt limits countries’ ability to borrow to close financing gaps. Countries are therefore left increasingly exposed to shocks, with minimal fiscal and financial buffers.

Sound fiscal and debt policies are central to preparing for, responding to, and recovering from external shocks. Fiscal buffers and debt sustainability determine the extent to which countries can absorb shocks and support recovery. Countries that entered shock episodes with adequate fiscal buffers, manageable debt levels, and a track record of countercyclical policies consistently limited long-term output losses. By contrast, high debt and procyclical spending amplified the economic damage.4 The interaction of limited fiscal buffers, elevated debt vulnerabilities, and weak policy execution points to three interconnected priorities: revenue mobilization and maintaining sound debt management, adopting countercyclical fiscal strategies, and investing in fiscal institutions.

Mobilizing revenue and managing debt. Revenue mobilization is not simply a matter of raising tax rates. Effective mobilization requires a holistic approach that strengthens the policy, administrative, and legal foundations of the tax system in tandem (Benitez et al. 2023). Without this broader institutional underpinning, additional revenue efforts risk being partial, inequitable, or unsustainable, undermining the fiscal resilience they are intended to build.

Effective debt management requires not only controlling the overall level of debt but also managing its composition and risk profile, including maturity, currency, interest rate, refinancing, and creditor risks. Sound debt management acts as a key shock absorber during times of crisis. Poor borrowing choices made during periods of stress can worsen liquidity and solvency risks, particularly when governments turn to short-term solutions that are less transparent or less market based, such as private placements or collateralized borrowing. These instruments may provide immediate financing, but they can also increase rollover risks, reduce transparency, constrain future policy choices, and expose public assets or future revenues to claims.

Governments should therefore design, implement, and communicate contingent borrowing plans before crises occur.

Conducting fiscal policy over the economic cycle. Economies that ran procyclical spending policies and persistent deficits over time faced economically larger and longer-lasting output losses from external shocks, whereas those that maintained countercyclical spending and ran primary surpluses, on average, experienced little to no losses. Dependence on commodities for exports and fiscal revenues makes commodity-exporting LMICs particularly exposed to swings in commodity prices.

Box 2.3 External Shocks and Fiscal Consolidation
Fiscal consolidation following a major external shock is particularly difficult and less likely to preserve growth. For example, consolidation episodes preceded by terms-of-trade shocks were significantly less successful in maintaining per capita growth rates near preconsolidation rates than episodes that were not preceded by such a shock (figure B2.3.1). This result reflects not only policy choices but also the persistent economic damage caused by the shock and the need for governments to support vulnerable households and economic activity before adjustment can begin.

Consolidation is often delayed even after fiscal balances become unsustainable, which carries compounding costs. Where the primary deficit was significantly larger than what would stabilize debt, countries tended to wait three to four years before embarking on meaningful fiscal consolidation (figure B2.3.2; Di Lorenzo and Lacey 2024). Political and social constraints are particularly binding in the aftermath of a shock, but delay can compound the eventual costs. Where large sustainability gaps (that is, the primary deficit was significantly larger than what would stabilize debt) persisted for four years or more, the median debt ratio increased by 17 percentage points of gross domestic product.

Growth also weakened: during periods of sustained fiscal unsustainability, average real gross domestic product per capita growth fell to the 32nd percentile of each country’s own historical distribution. For countries facing high borrowing costs and limited market access, these findings underscore the value of early, credible, and growth-conscious corrective action.

During commodity price booms and the resulting rise in fiscal revenues, governments in those economies tend to increase spending. Without primary surpluses, those economies tend to have fewer fiscal resources to support activity and protect vulnerable populations when external shocks hit. Increased spending and debt accumulation during booms may also lead to a loss of market confidence during commodity price busts, requiring a large fiscal adjustment or contributing to debt distress (refer to box 2.3 for more details on external shocks and fiscal consolidation). The implication is clear: fiscal strategies that save windfalls during economic upturns, such as commodity booms, and deploy those savings during downturns allow governments to respond effectively when shocks arrive.

Establishing credible fiscal institutions and fiscal buffers. When a shock hits, the fiscal impact can be immediate and large, as spending needed to protect vulnerable communities rises while revenues fall. Governments can prepare for this tendency by establishing contingency reserves within the annual budget, natural disaster funds with clear rules governing their use and size calibrated to historical experience, and state-contingent debt instruments and other insurance mechanisms that transfer a portion of disaster risk to third parties (Polacek 2018). Well-designed fiscal rules can reinforce these buffers while allowing temporary, transparent flexibility during severe shocks. These instruments should be integrated into broader fiscal risk and debt-management frameworks.

Food Import Exposure, External Debt Burdens, and Healthy Diet Affordability
Food imports are an important channel through which external shocks can affect food and nutrition security. They are particularly relevant as countries face an uncertain external environment, with geopolitical tensions, weather-related shocks, trade disruptions, and volatility in energy and fertilizer markets posing continued risks to global food markets and prices (FAO 2026; World Bank 2026a). Such shocks may be especially difficult to absorb in economies with high external debt burdens.

Food Import Shares in Poorer Economies
Across the sample, which consists predominantly of LMICs, the share of food in merchandise imports generally declines as income per capita rises (figure 2.13, panel a). By contrast, economies with larger external debt burdens relative to exports also tend to have higher food import shares (figure 2.13, panel b).5 Both relationships matter for an economy’s capacity to manage food import exposure. Lower-income economies may have less room to absorb increases in import costs, and a high debt-to-exports ratio indicates that external debt is large relative to export earnings.

text: During external shocks, higher import costs can therefore coincide with weaker economic and external buffers; export earnings may also decline, further increasing pressure on foreign exchange resources and raising the debt-to-exports ratio, even without an increase in the debt stock. Import Reliance and Debt Burdens Across Food Groups Aggregate food import shares do not show how strongly the domestic supply of individual food groups depends on international markets. Net import reliance— net imports as a share of domestic supply quantity—varies substantially across the six food groups making up the Healthy Diet Basket (Bai, Herforth et al. 2025; Herforth et al. 2025).

Median reliance is lower for animal-source foods, at 28.0 percent, and for vegetables and fruits, at 17.4 percent and 13.4 percent, respectively.

Diversifying Import Sources to Improve Resilience
Import reliance, however, captures only one dimension of exposure. Another is how concentrated imports are across source economies. An economy that sources a food group from a broader range of suppliers may have more options to adjust when trade with a particular exporter is disrupted than one that depends on only a few sources. Import source diversity is measured using the Shannon Diversity Index,7 which captures both the number of source economies and how evenly imports are distributed across them; higher values indicate greater diversification. Higher-income economies generally source food imports from a broader and more evenly distributed set of suppliers (Bai, Kaushik et al. 2025).

text: During 2017–19, the relationship between changes in healthy diet unaffordability and external debt burdens was weak and not statistically significant. In these periods, economies with higher debt stocks relative to export earnings tended to experience larger increases, or smaller declines, in healthy diet unaffordability. A doubling of the debt-to-exports ratio was associated with a more adverse change in unaffordability of approximately 1.6–1.8 percentage points. During 2023–25, the relationship weakened again and was no longer statistically significant.

metadata.section: Food Import Exposure, External Debt Burdens, and Healthy Diet Affordability

text: As revealed in this section, food import vulnerability reflects both reliance on imported supply and the concentration of import sources, and these dimensions can coincide with high external debt burdens. The period analysis adds an outcome perspective, showing that higher debt burdens are more strongly associated with nutrition security challenges during major external shocks, as reflected in changes in healthy diet unaffordability. This pattern is consistent with the earlier framing of debt acting as an amplifier of vulnerability, and it highlights the importance of considering food import exposure and external debt together when assessing a country’s nutrition resilience to future external shocks.
