text:
Introduction
Over the past five years, the debt transparency agenda has moved decisively from an aspiration to a reality, translating commitments into tangible improvements in the coverage, accuracy, timeliness, and usability of debt data. This progress comes at a critical moment. As the prior chapters of this report show, the external debt stock of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and the costs of servicing that debt are at a record high, putting increasing pressure on public finances in many LMICs and crowding out critical social and development spending.

In this environment, strengthening debt transparency is not merely a statistical objective; instead, it is an essential foundation for sound fiscal management, effective risk assessment, informed policy making, and financial stability.

This chapter charts the progress made to date to enhance debt transparency in LMICs and discusses the important initiatives currently under way to scale up the debt transparency agenda.

Progress in Debt Transparency, 2020–25
Debt transparency is at the center of the World Bank Group’s engagement with its borrowers and partners. The policy commitment of the International Development Association (IDA) is to support debt sustainability and debt transparency through technical assistance, knowledge, and financing engagements.

The Sustainable Development Finance Policy (SDFP), which became effective in July 2020, requires IDA-eligible borrowers at moderate or elevated risk of debt distress to take concrete policy performance actions (PPAs) to enhance debt transparency, strengthen debt management, and promote fiscal sustainability.1 These PPAs have been instrumental in incentivizing countries to embrace sustainable development financing, embed debt transparency reforms into national policy frameworks, and institutionalize transparent disclosure of public debt data.

The policy also leverages IDA’s global convening capacity to foster closer coordination among creditors to mitigate debt-related vulnerabilities, which has facilitated the reconciliation of data reported by borrowers to the World Bank Group Debtor Reporting System (DRS) with data made available by bilateral creditors. Consequently, asymmetries between the two data sets have

narrowed, further enhancing the coverage and accuracy of LMICs’ external debt data published by the World Bank Group in International Debt Statistics. Since the SDFP policy became effective, a total of 887 PPAs have been agreed, of which 60 percent focused on debt transparency and debt management and 40 percent on fiscal sustainability. In its first year in operation, fiscal year (FY) 2021, 55 IDA countries committed to 130 PPAs. By FY2026, these numbers had risen to 65 IDA countries implementing 159 PPAs, of which 55 percent focused on debt transparency and debt management. During the initial years of implementation, PPAs related to debt transparency focused on foundational measures aimed at disclosure of timely and comprehensive debt bulletins.

More recently, the focus has shifted to monitoring and disclosure of contingent liabilities, borrowing by state-owned enterprises (SOEs), and actions that institutionalize timely debt monitoring and reporting. Overall, PPAs related to debt transparency have fallen from 32 percent of total PPAs in FY2021 to 10 percent in FY2026, reflecting progress made in disclosure of debt data. However, the sustained implementation of reform measures in some IDA countries has proved challenging, particularly in states categorized as fragile and conflict affected.

In addition, with tighter global financing conditions, some governments have turned to off-budget and increasingly complex debt instruments—including bilateral currency swaps, total return swaps, and collateralized loans—to meet financing needs, making it harder to assess public debt exposure.

The SDFP has consistently prioritized debt management, and the share of PPAs in debt management has remained steady, rising from 41 percent of total PPAs in FY2021 to 45 percent in FY2026. Debt management PPAs address risks stemming from high debt levels by ensuring compliance with nonconcessional borrowing ceilings. They also focus on strengthening institutional structures for debt management, including the creation of dedicated debt offices, strong legal and governance frameworks, and enhanced procedures for managing sovereign guarantees, on-lending, and borrowing by SOEs. Future PPAs in debt management will continue to address gaps in legislative frameworks, institutional fragmentation, and inadequate oversight of public borrowing.

The SDFP also plays a catalytic role in advancing reforms related to the management of domestic debt and the development of domestic debt markets. These reforms have included PPAs that supported the formulation and publication of medium-term debt strategies with clear targets for domestic and external borrowing in Fiji, the Kyrgyz Republic, Nigeria, the Solomon Islands, and Sri Lanka, and publication of annual borrowing plans that include domestic borrowing in the Central African Republic, Côte d’Ivoire, and St. Lucia. PPAs have also supported the development of operational guidelines for the issuance of government bonds in the domestic market in Bangladesh, the Solomon Islands, and Tonga; the strengthening of

investor relations in Togo; the publication of calendars for domestic bond issuance in Kosovo and Liberia; and measures to improve recording of domestic debt liabilities in Comoros.

Going forward, the SDFP can play an even more critical role in advancing reforms to support domestic borrowing and development of investor relations and the implementation of a comprehensive legal and regulatory framework to govern domestic debt issuance, including clear delineation of the roles of the ministry of finance and the central bank. With IDA countries grappling with high debt burdens, rising financing needs, and a complex financing environment with options for riskier external financing arrangements, sound debt management of total public debt liabilities is more critical than ever.

The World Bank Group tracks progress in borrowing countries’ public debt dissemination practices on an annual basis. Its assessment of these outcomes is presented in a heat map that measures the strengths and weaknesses of the dissemination practices in 76 IDA-eligible countries across nine key indicators: data accessibility, instrument coverage, sectoral coverage, information on recently contracted external loans, periodicity, time lag, debt management strategy, annual borrowing plan, and additional statistics and memo items.2 The Debt Reporting Heat Map shows that, over the past five years, IDA-eligible borrowers have made significant progress in public debt disclosure practices.

In 2020, only 36 IDA-eligible countries, 47 percent of the 76 countries covered by the heat map, published fully accessible public debt data. The 2025 heat map found that 54 countries, or 72 percent, had fully accessible public debt data, a 25-percentage-point gain from 2020 (figure 3.1). Data accessibility in Sub-Saharan African countries has also improved significantly, rising from 19 countries (50 percent of countries in the region) that published fully accessible data in 2020, to 29 countries (or 76 percent) in 2025 despite a regression in accessibility of data in some countries.

These countries include Ethiopia, where data accessibility had deteriorated since it defaulted on its international bond in 2023, and Senegal, following the revelation by the auditors of a large understatement in the official debt statistics. Even in countries that have accessible data, important information gaps persist. Instrument coverage has improved, with 45 countries assessed as having full coverage in 2025 compared to 33 countries in 2020, but progress has been slower than accessibility. Additionally, comprehensive sector coverage is limited, with subnational borrowing, contingent liabilities, and the obligations of SOE debt often excluded from the official public debt figure.
Moreover, only about one-quarter of countries report instrument-level information on the terms of newly contracted debt.

Improvements in data accessibility identified by the heat map are mirrored in enhanced timeliness and accuracy of reporting to the World Bank Group DRS. This is a mandatory reporting requirement for all countries that borrow from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) and IDA. Borrowers are increasingly meeting this requirement in accordance with the reporting timetable and are providing more comprehensive information on borrowing by central banks and SOEs.

These advances have reduced gaps and asymmetries in global debt statistics, strengthened cross-country comparability, and solidified the DRS role as a cornerstone of global debt transparency.

For the end-2025 data reporting round, only 5.8 percent of the 121 LMICs obligated to report to the DRS missed the end-June 2026 deadline or failed to report, and most of those countries were at war or in conflict. This is a marked improvement over 2020, when 13 percent of countries were late reporters or nonreporters. Countries are also reporting earlier in the cycle, with 82 percent of countries submitting the end-2025 report by end- April—that is, only a four-month lag—which represents a 14-percentage-point increase from 2020 when 68 percent of countries reported by end-April (figure 3.2).

Significant progress has been made to improve the quality, coverage, and consistency of external debt statistics through systematic debtor-creditor reconciliation exercises. At the core of this initiative is the reconciliation of loan-by-loan information on public and publicly guaranteed external debt reported by borrowers to the DRS with corresponding data provided by bilateral creditors. This process enables cross-checking of data sets, identification of discrepancies, validation of loan terms and transactions, and filling of critical data gaps, all of which serve to enhance the accuracy of debt statistics.

Initiated in 2022, these exercises have become a central element of the broader debt transparency agenda, supporting more accurate debt monitoring, improved data validation, and better-informed debt analysis in IDA-eligible countries. The first reconciliation exercise, conducted using end-2021 data, covered 3,655 individual loans and loan tranches reported by 18 creditor countries, including all Group of Seven (G-7) members and 11 Paris Club creditors. Approximately 80 percent of loans were successfully matched, representing about 90 percent of total outstanding debt values, providing a first comprehensive assessment of discrepancies between debtor and creditor records.

Despite a remaining overall difference of about 10 percent, the exercise provided critical insights into the nature and sources of discrepancies and established a strong foundation for future rounds.

The third and most recent round of the reconciliation exercise, using end-2024 data, demonstrated substantial progress in aligning the debtor and creditor data sets for both scale and accuracy. Again, 18 creditors participated and together reported 4,875 individual loans and loan tranches, representing $63.4 billion in outstanding debt, out of which a total of 3,762 loans and loan tranches (77 percent) were matched to their counterpart in the DRS database (figure 3.3). For matched loans, creditor-reported claims of $58.0 billion differed by less than 1 percent from the comparable figure reported by debtors to the DRS, indicating that remaining gaps are relatively limited in magnitude.

The overall reporting gap, equivalent to $5.4 billion, masks much wider variations for individual creditors, but the reconciliation exercise found that gaps are also progressively narrowing. Figure 3.4 compares the total end-2024 claims reported by each of the 18 creditors with the total debt owed to each creditor that debtors reported to the DRS. Points on the dashed line indicate perfect alignment between debtor and creditor reporting. For 6 of the 18 participating creditors, the end-2024 claims align fully with the comparable figure reported by borrowers to the DRS, and for 2 creditors the gap was small.

For other creditors, where larger differences were observed, these differences were typically concentrated in a small number of loans and found to be primarily the result of misclassification or differences in reporting norms, not true errors. As the chart also shows, discrepancies are not one directional: points above the dashed line indicate that claims reported by the creditor are higher than the comparable amount reported by the debtor, and points below the line reflect cases where the debtor figure is higher than the creditor. The reconciliation exercises have highlighted that asymmetries between debtor and creditor data are not driven solely by gaps in debtor country reporting.

Rather, they arise from several factors including differences in definitions, reporting practices, and institutional coordination. On the debtor side, these factors include (a) weak debt management, which limits timely, comprehensive recording of debt liabilities; (b) time lags in reporting new commitments and disbursements; (c) understatement of arrears, particularly penalty interest charges, often due to the complexity of how these are calculated; (d) failure to report, which results in estimated data by World Bank Group staff; and (e) misclassification of direct and guaranteed export credits.

Creditor-side factors include (a) lack of standard methodology and variation in national accounting norms; (b) the practice of some creditors to record disbursements as loan tranches without reference to the original loan commitment; (c) potential double-counting of bilateral lending delivered through common funds such as the European Economic Community–IDA trust fund and captured in the DRS as multilateral debt; and (d) inclusion of claims that are not external public sector, such as loans to private sector entities.

Other reasons for asymmetries between the debtor and creditor data include recording of indemnification of payment arrears to private creditors on guaranteed export credits typically captured in debtor data only when a formal debt restructuring takes place. This problem is compounded by the fact that most creditors do not publish information on loans they have guaranteed. There is also an absence of a standard methodology applicable to both debtors and creditors for recording forgiveness of bilateral claims and bilateral debt swaps that extinguish external debt obligations in return for investment of the local currency equivalent in a dedicated fund for specific expenditures such as education or measures to mitigate climate change.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: The reconciliation process has strengthened dialogue and underscored mutual accountability and the need for standardized reporting frameworks. Currently, DRS submissions provide more granular and complete information—such as loan-level details, disbursements, and terms—which are not always fully mirrored in creditor data sets. At the same time, the reconciliation exercises have played a critical role in identifying persistent data gaps, particularly regarding the liabilities of SOEs and structural weaknesses in debt reporting systems.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: Since the reconciliation process began, tangible progress has taken place in creditor engagement. An increasing number of creditors provided a detailed response to follow-up queries and provided data clarification, contributing to more accurate gap-filling and reconciliation outcomes, reflecting a transition toward systematic collaboration. Building on this momentum will be critical to resolving remaining discrepancies and ensuring that the reconciliation exercise continues to deliver sustained improvements in data quality, transparency, and comparability.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text:
Overall, these data-sharing and reconciliation efforts have already significantly narrowed asymmetries between borrower and creditor data, strengthened the credibility of debt statistics, and improved the analytical foundation for monitoring debt vulnerabilities. As discussed in the following sections, continued collaboration, expanded participation, and ongoing methodological enhancements are expected to further advance data quality, transparency, and global comparability of debt statistics.

text: foreign currency obligations and assess creditworthiness, it evolved into a global public good, International Debt Statistics (IDS), which plays a central role in promoting debt transparency through the provision of standardized, cross-country comparable information on external debt levels in LMICs. Together, the DRS and the IDS are the backbone of the World Bank Group’s debt transparency architecture.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text:
Building a New Generation of Debt Statistics
The DRS collects detailed, instrument-level information on public and publicly guaranteed external debt from IBRD and IDA borrowers to support the operational work of the World Bank Group. This work includes debt sustainability analysis, country diagnostics, debt transparency assessments, technical assistance, reform programs, and policy dialogue on macroeconomic outcomes and goals. Through its long-standing engagement with national debt offices, ministries of finance, and central banks, the DRS has become the central platform for methodological alignment, data validation, and institutional strengthening.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: The IDS, the World Bank Group’s flagship statistical database on external debt, underpins the annual publication of the International Debt Report and serves as the primary global repository of external debt data for LMICs. It draws on data reported to the DRS and complementary information from other sources, including multilateral and bilateral creditors, international financial institutions, market data, and other statistical data sets to create the world’s most comprehensive and globally comparable statistical resource for policy makers, investors, researchers, and development partners.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: (Refer to annex 3A for more information on sources of debt statistics.) Complementary databases updated quarterly—Quarterly External Debt Statistics and Quarterly Public Sector Debt— provide high-frequency data that support the monitoring of evolving debt trends for the current year.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text:
Modernizing and Expanding the DRS
The DRS is currently undergoing the most extensive makeover since it was first implemented in the 1950s. The rationale for this modernization and expansion is threefold. The process aims to (a) introduce a new reporting framework and more comprehensive instrument-level reporting that responds to the changes in the global financial architecture and multiplicity of borrowing instruments now available to LMICs; (b) bring DRS reporting norms into conformity with the most recent international standards and definitions for recording and compiling debt statistics; and (c) take advantage of the latest advances in technology, including

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: where appropriate artificial intelligence, to streamline and simplify the reporting process, assist reporters with queries about reporting protocols, and validate the consistency of data. The new DRS framework, which will be finalized and rolled out in the coming year, represents a major step forward in strengthening the global debt data architecture.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: The reporting framework is being expanded to introduce more comprehensive instrument-level reporting, including additional information on loan characteristics, debtor and creditor guarantees, collateral arrangements, debt reorganization, creditor attributes, and emerging financing instruments such as total return swaps, third party discounted buybacks, and asset-backed financing. The reporting requirements are designed to capture a comprehensive and much richer picture of all the basic characteristics of each debt instrument, such as borrower, lender, and associated terms. For example, additional reporting fields require the reporter to provide information on the type of debt security and the market and nominal value at the end of each reporting period.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: This information facilitates a more comprehensive analysis, such as an evaluation of the impact of market fluctuations on the valuation of debt instruments and alignment and comparison with the international statistical standards, in this case the liabilities recorded by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) International Investment Position. The reporting standards and definitions are aligned to the latest international statistical standards, including the revised IMF directives on the compilation of balance of payments statistics from the seventh edition of the IMF’s Integrated Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (IMF 2025) and the United Nations Statistics Division’s 2025 System of National Accounts.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: The new state-of-the-art DRS platform represents a radical change from the prior mechanism for the collection and compilation of debt data. It is structured around three key modules: data collection, data management, and reporting and analytics that take full advantage of the latest technological developments. The platform is designed to meet several key objectives: simplify and improve reporting efficiency for borrowers; incorporate automated data validation processes; enhance analytical capabilities; and facilitate greater interoperability with other international statistical systems.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: The development of the new DRS platform and its rollout are being coordinated with the Commonwealth Secretariat (Meridian) and the Debt Management and Financial Analysis System of UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), which provide the debt management software currently used by about 80 percent of DRS reporting countries. The goal is a seamless extraction, validation, and automated pass-through of data recorded by the borrowers in these systems to

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: the World Bank Group in a format that meets the DRS reporting requirement. The modernization of the DRS will also expand users’ access to IDS and allow them to generate customized aggregates and conduct deeper analytical work, while preserving the strict confidentiality of instrument-level information that borrowers share with the World Bank Group.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: With the new reporting mechanism, DRS reporters will submit data through a web-based portal that streamlines and facilitates compliance with the World Bank Group reporting requirements. It provides reporters with an easy-to-use and efficient method for submitting both data and metadata securely. Reporting is structured around one reporting template that includes both public and publicly guaranteed and private nonguaranteed external debt and complementary modules, which replace the collective of DRS reporting forms previously used. The new portal enables DRS reporters to download the standardized reporting template and the related modules, and to upload data and validate them for consistency before submission to the World Bank Group.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: To facilitate reporting, it also includes a hyperlink to the DRS reporting manual and online how-to guidance for reporters when the reporting validating mechanism flags inconsistencies in the data being uploaded by the reporter.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text:
Integrating Domestic Public Debt into the Debt Transparency Agenda
A critical new frontier for the debt transparency agenda is the expansion of data coverage to domestic public debt, which has become an increasingly important share of LMICs’ public debt. In many of these countries, domestic public debt now accounts for 40–60 percent of total public debt, and in some of them it exceeds those shares. Despite the centrality of domestic debt levels to fiscal sustainability, sound monetary policy, and financial stability, data on domestic debt obligations remain fragmented, inconsistently defined, and only partially captured in international data sets.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: In marked contrast to external public debt, no comprehensive global platform currently exists to systematically collect and disseminate detailed, comprehensive, and cross-country comparable domestic public debt data for LMICs.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: The World Bank Group initiative to extend the DRS to domestic public debt represents a unique contribution to the global data architecture. It is the only framework currently in development that aims to bring together detailed, standardized, and cross-country comparable domestic public debt statistics for LMICs. The integration of domestic and external debt into a single, coherent reporting system to the DRS opens the door, for the first time, to the creation of a comprehensive and unified picture of public sector liabilities. This picture will provide the wherewithal to make a far more accurate assessment of a

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: country’s debt sustainability and an evaluation of the fiscal risks domestic debt obligations pose.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: This initiative presents institutional and technical challenges. Extensive diagnostic work, including surveys and pilot exercises conducted by the World Bank Group with DRS reporting countries and partner institutions that support them— including the IMF, the Commonwealth Secretariat, and UNCTAD—identified a vast and complex array of instruments for raising financing in domestic markets. In many LMICs, domestic debt is managed by multiple entities, including ministries of finance, central banks, and subnational governments, and recorded in different systems using a variety of classifications. An important element of the new reporting framework will be the introduction of a standardized reporting template based on international definitions and classifications.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: It will be complemented by a detailed reporting manual and comprehensive guidelines on consolidation of domestic and external public debt across different levels of government to derive comprehensive and accurate measures of total public sector liabilities. To support implementation, the World Bank Group is developing methodological guidance on compiling and reporting domestic debt statistics in collaboration with the IMF, the Commonwealth Secretariat, UNCTAD, and other international partners.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: Implementation of the domestic debt module represents a major expansion of the DRS and will require significant institutional reforms and technical enhancements in many LMICs. These changes include strengthening legal mandates for data collection, improving coordination across public sector entities, and upgrading debt management systems. In view of these needs, the domestic debt reporting framework will be introduced on a phased and voluntary basis, beginning with central government debt and progressively expanding to full public sector coverage, thereby allowing LMICs to participate according to their capacity while simultaneously benefiting from targeted technical assistance.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text:
The World Bank Group is confident that, over time, full integration of domestic and external debt data into a unified reporting framework can be achieved with a game-changing impact on debt transparency. Comprehensive debt statistics will provide critical insights into total public debt burdens, maturity concentration, interest rate exposure, and rollover risks, and will enhance the reconciliation of debt records with fiscal and monetary statistics and overall macroeconomic surveillance.

Institutionalizing Debtor-Creditor Data Sharing and Reconciliation
The debtor-creditor reconciliation exercise has become an annual program supported by continuous and structured engagement with participating

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: G-7 and Paris Club creditors. As already illustrated, these reconciliation exercises have been instrumental in improving data-sharing practices, enhancing methodological alignment, and expanding the scope and coverage of the exercise. The reconciliation of data reported by debtors to the DRS with the comparable creditor records has played a critical role in identifying structural data gaps and has demonstrated how detailed loan-level data sharing and dialogue can lead to tangible results, including the resolution of large discrepancies and the closing of previously unreported debt positions. These results have also reinforced the need for continuous dialogue and data reconciliation, and adoption of standardized reporting norms to sustain concordance between debtor and creditor data.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text:
Efforts are already under way to broaden participation beyond the
current group of G-7 and Paris Club bilateral creditors. Ongoing discussions with key Group of Twenty creditors are positive, and the expectation is that additional bilateral creditors will participate in the next end-2025 data reconciliation exercise. In this context, an important development is the publication in July 2026 by the World Bank Group Chief Statistician of the “Protocol on the Handling of Creditor Data Submitted to the World Bank Debtor Reporting System” (Chief Statistician 2026). It sets out the terms on which these data are shared and the confidentiality rules that apply to them, providing reassurance for creditors that the data will be used strictly for purposes of data reconciliation.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: This has been an important factor in the creditors’ decision to share the very detailed information required for the reconciliation exercise. Over time, the plan is to extend participation to all official creditors, both bilateral and multilateral, and to encourage private creditors to participate.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text:
The World Bank Group is actively engaged in devising mechanisms to
streamline and automate the reconciliation process (refer to box 3.1 on the Indonesia Loan Clearing Module Pilot Project). There is also a proposal to integrate a creditor reporting module into the DRS cloud-based platform to enable creditors to submit data electronically and securely. This capability would replace the current email-based submission process and significantly improve the efficiency, standardization, and security of creditor reporting. In parallel, the creditor reporting template is being redefined to capture more granular information, particularly on loan terms, transactions, guarantees, and restructuring details.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text: These details are already made available to the DRS by debtors, and the objective is to enhance comparability across the data sets and eliminate all discrepancies.

metadata.section: Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda

text:
Box 3.1 The Indonesia Loan Clearing Module Pilot Project
New standards and protocols for debt data reconciliation supported by innovative information technology solutions to systematically digitalize and automatically reconcile public loan data have the potential to ensure better quality recording and save time and effort. The World Bank Group is already evaluating such standards and protocols. In 2025, it launched a pilot project in Indonesia, funded by the Japanese Ministry of Finance, to develop a Loan Clearing Module to facilitate information sharing between borrowers and official creditors. This module acts as a platform for information sharing between creditors’ data systems and those of local debt management offices.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: For each new transaction (that is, new loan signed, payment, disbursement, or modification), the originator would create a new data file electronically transmitted to the platform according to standardized templates. The counterpart then validates the information and automatically transfers the data as needed into its own debt recording system. In its first phase, this project seeks to reconcile loans issued by Indonesia’s largest external lenders (the Japan International Cooperation Agency, the Asian Development Bank, and the World Bank Group), before including a wider group of Indonesian official and potential private sector creditors in the second phase.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: Implementation of the pilot project in Indonesia has already demonstrated the technical feasibility of continuous synchronization and validation of debtor and creditor data. The debt office has already automatically transferred World Bank Group loan data and uploaded them into the local debt system; as of May 2026, the platform had successfully exchanged and validated a total of 761 loan records, and 642 subefforts are under way to cover other official creditors. Once fully operational, the Loan Clearing Module codes could be made available to other countries, potentially serving as an international platform for debt data reconciliation, providing a new, real-time source of fully validated debt statistics.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text:
Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency
Debt transparency involves much more than encouraging debtors and their creditors to disclose additional data. Advancing the debt transparency agenda ultimately depends on strengthening loan records, disbursement records, and payment records. Producing accurate and comprehensive data to the standard required for informed fiscal and debt management decision-making requires strong institutional arrangements, rigorous legal and governance structures, consistent statistical standards, and robust validation processes.

Building the Foundations of Debt Transparency
Capacity building is an integral part of the World Bank Group’s debt transparency agenda. Over the past five years, the Debt Statistics Team has

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: contributed to 23 courses and workshops at the global, regional, and country levels. These opportunities were complemented by targeted technical assistance for individual IDA-eligible countries and continuous engagement with other international organizations and regional banks providing comparable capacity-building services. Support from the Debt Statistics Team is broad-based and includes presentations on best practice in monitoring and recording debt data, advice on how to manage the public debt portfolio and contingent liabilities, and guidance for understanding and adopting international statistical standards and definitions.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: This support is combined with assistance on how to strengthen institutional systems and human resources responsible for compilation and dissemination of debt statistics at the national level and to international data sets. It also builds awareness on how these data factor into decision-making regarding public borrowing and debt sustainability within the broader framework of macroeconomic policies. The delivery mechanism has also evolved with a heightened emphasis on practical training aimed at strengthening the entire debt data production chain.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: This training includes all aspects of the data collection process, from recording individual debt instruments, to institutional coordination to monitor stocks and flows, data validation and reconciliation, and dissemination and use of comprehensive debt statistics for analyses and use by policy makers.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: The modernization and expansion of the DRS serves as an important anchor for structuring the capacity-building program in debt data management. It currently covers about 120 World Bank Group borrowing countries and more than 50,000 active loan records, with approximately 2,500–3,000 new loans reported each year. Maintaining a system of this scale and ensuring the integrity of the data require sustained investment in national reporting capacity. Practical training sessions are not limited to familiarizing debt managers with the new and very different DRS reporting structure. They include equally, if not more, important training in how to implement international statistical standards to categorize and compile debt data.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: In this context, the overarching goal is to also transmit the skills required to determine if data are complete, internally consistent, appropriately classified, and aligned with international statistical standards. Workshops provide hands-on experience and test runs of the revised classifications and reporting requirements, and explain the links between DRS concepts and External Debt Statistics: Guide for Compilers and Users (IMF 2014). Such alignments are important because countries should not have to maintain parallel conceptual frameworks for national external debt statistics and international reporting.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: Moreover, consistency between the two reduces the reporting burden, improves comparability, and enhances the use of DRS data for the countries’ own debt management and analytical purposes.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: The agenda is also expanding beyond external debt. The voluntary rollout of reporting on domestic public debt creates an opportunity to strengthen countries’ capacity to produce a more comprehensive picture of total public sector indebtedness. Over time, this capacity can help reduce the historical divide between external and domestic debt reporting, and support more integrated analysis of countries’ overall debt vulnerabilities.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text:
A Partnership-Based Model to Develop Capacity
The World Bank Group’s approach to capacity building to strengthen debt management is multifaceted and includes regional courses, country-specific technical assistance, and peer learning delivered in partnerships with other international organizations. Regional workshops are typically organized as intensive five-day programs combining technical presentations with exercises, country cases, simulations, and structured discussions. They allow participants to apply statistical concepts to the practical problems they encounter in their daily work.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: Participation extends beyond debt management offices, and the World Bank Group strives to bring together, whenever possible, staff from central banks, ministries of finance, statistical agencies, and other institutions involved in producing debt information. This cross-institutional approach is important because weaknesses in debt statistics often arise not from a lack of information but from fragmentation of that information across multiple government institutions. Bringing these institutions together can improve understanding of responsibilities, facilitate data sharing, and strengthen consistency across national data sets.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: Partnerships with institutions like the IMF, the Commonwealth Secretariat, and UNCTAD strengthen the multifaceted approach by contributing to regional training programs, connecting statistical standards to debt management practices and reporting requirements, and underscoring the imperatives of ensuring debt data management systems are updated and validated on a daily basis. Cooperation with the Commonwealth Secretariat and UNCTAD is particularly valuable now, as the redesigned DRS is being incorporated into the debt management systems they have created and maintain in order to embed methodological changes into national operating environments and to automate DRS reporting requirements.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text:
Responding to an Increasingly Complex Debt Landscape
Capacity building has also expanded to address areas where weaknesses in coverage can have significant implications for assessments of public debt and fiscal risks. One such area is nonguaranteed borrowing by SOEs and other public sector entities. Identifying these liabilities can be difficult when information is dispersed across institutions or when debt management systems focus primarily on central government borrowing. Training therefore helps participants identify

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: institutional coverage gaps and understand how nonguaranteed and contingent liabilities should be captured and classified. More attention is also being given to emerging and complex instruments. As sovereign financing evolves and lending instruments become more complex, methodological guidance on how to account for them and expertise in assessing the risks they may pose takes on added importance.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: An important evolution in the capacity-building program has been its integration into the World Bank Group’s mainstream work on data quality and debt sustainability. Data discrepancies are increasingly being seen not simply as errors to be corrected but as diagnostic information that offers insights into weaknesses in national systems. The annual reconciliation of debtor and creditor information is a good example. Differences may reveal problems in creditor classification, exchange rate conversion, recording of arrears, treatment of restructurings, institutional coverage, or the timing of transactions. Working through these discrepancies directly with country authorities provides an opportunity to identify their causes and improve compilation practices at the source.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: The same principle underpins the work of harmonizing the data to the DRS and the data national authorities provide for the debt sustainability analyses conducted jointly by the IMF and the World Bank Group. Improvements in the timeliness and quality of reporting to the DRS by IDA-eligible countries offer clear indications that these measures are having a positive knock-on effect.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text:
Providing Continuous and Scalable Learning
Traditional face-to-face training is valuable and essential, particularly where participants need to work through country-specific institutional and methodological issues. But the scale of training required, coupled with the turnover of staff in national debt offices, is such that capacity building cannot be delivered exclusively through periodic workshops. The next phase is therefore moving toward a more continuous model combining regional training, targeted technical assistance, methodological guidance, and digital learning.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text:
Training materials are being developed in conjunction with the updated DRS Manual and reporting guidance, and collaboration with the World Bank Group Data Academy can provide structured e-learning modules that countries can access between formal training events.

This approach can create a more sustainable capacity-building ecosystem with introductory modules providing a common foundation for new debt compilers and specialized modules to address topics such as restructuring, arrears, contingent liabilities, creditor classification, domestic debt, and new financial instruments. Online tools such as validation guides and step-by-step guides to reporting templates, test exercises, and case studies can support participants

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: after formal training has ended. This support will enable regional or country workshops to focus on practical applications and more complex cases and create the space for peer learning, which will remain an important part of this model. Countries frequently face similar challenges, and regional workshops provide an opportunity to exchange practical solutions and institutional experiences that cannot easily be captured in manuals. Group exercises and simulations have demonstrated the value of allowing participants to work jointly through real reporting and classification problems.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text:
From Capacity Building to Sustainable Debt Transparency
Success is not measured by the number of people trained but by the improvement in the coverage, quality, and transparency of the debt data countries produce. It requires institutional and instrument coverage, more timely submissions, fewer unexplained discrepancies, better reconciliation between national and international data sets, and greater public availability of debt information, and can be achieved only by tailoring and adapting capacity-building activities to country circumstances and needs.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: For some countries, the primary need is methodological training; for others, it centers on institutional improvements in debt management systems, assistance in reconciling databases, or extending coverage of public sector debt to SOEs, contingent liabilities, or domestic debt. Diagnostic information from DRS reporting, data validation, debtor-creditor reconciliation, and comparisons with other international data sets are increasingly being used to target technical assistance to areas where they will have the greatest impact. The World Bank Group’s role extends beyond collecting debt data, to supporting LMICs to build the human capital and institutional arrangements and the systems required to produce them.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: Sustainable improvements in debt transparency depend on strong national institutions with the capacity to generate reliable information.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: As both external and domestic financing for LMICs becomes more complex, this investment will become even more important. New creditors, new instruments, growing domestic debt markets, and greater attention to public sector and contingent liabilities are expanding the information countries need to manage them. Capacity building must evolve alongside these developments if borrowers are to keep pace. Ultimately, more reliable debt data and stronger national capacity go hand in hand and reinforce each other. More robust institutions produce better statistics, which in turn underscore inherent weaknesses and permit technical support to be targeted more effectively; and stronger national systems make improvements in debt transparency more durable.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text: Capacity building is not complementary to the debt transparency agenda; rather, it is one of the foundations on which the agenda stands.

metadata.section: Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency

text:
Debt Asymmetries
Transparent external and public debt data are fundamental to assessing LMICs’ financial situations. These data provide the foundation for debt sustainability analysis, managing fiscal and monetary policy, and disclosure of the level and composition of existing obligations to creditors, investors, development partners, and citizens. The expectation is that debt transparency will bring clarity with a definitive account of a country’s debt situation. All too often, however, the debt data disseminated by LMICs differ from creditors’ claims, raising doubts about data accuracy, under-recording, or, worse, deliberate nondisclosure and hidden debt.

Although these situations are sometimes the case, the primary challenge to the accuracy, credibility, and comparability of debt data is asymmetries, particularly between debtor- and creditor-reported figures.

Addressing Debt Asymmetries Is Key to Debt Transparency
Asymmetries in debt data arise primarily from inconsistent methodological definitions and accounting practices in debtor and creditor countries and other institutions that compile and disseminate debt data. These divergent practices present a minefield for users trying to compare debtor and creditor data or to make cross-country comparisons across groups of debtors or creditors. In extreme cases discrepancies as large as 30 percent of gross domestic product have been observed in debt stock figures purporting to have the same coverage.

Issues as simple as classification of domestic and external debt on a currency basis will likely result in a very different number for external debt stocks than the one disseminated by the World Bank Group in IDS, which uses the international standard residency criterion. Conversely, IDS may legitimately record a lower figure for external debt owed to a creditor than the creditor itself records. This discrepancy occurs because the IDS figure excludes loans to nonguaranteed private sector borrowers, not separately identifiable in the aggregate data reported to the DRS. Mitigating data asymmetries is key to being able to validate debt data and confirm those data to be comprehensive and accurate, a core objective of the debt transparency agenda.

The Reasons for Asymmetries in Debt Data
One of the key reasons for debt data asymmetries is the existence of multiple data sources. The primary sources are debtor and creditor accounting, and data collection frameworks. The main actors in debtor countries are debt management offices, finance ministries, central banks, and national statistical agencies, which have varying institutional mandates and data collection mechanisms. In creditor countries, there are the databases of bilateral lending agencies

such as aid ministries, official export credit agencies, and public sector banks. International financial institutions like the IMF and the World Bank Group are important creditors, and they play a central role in the compilation of global debt and other external sector statistics. Similarly, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) collects and disseminates data on aid flows and bilateral loans, and the Bank for International Settlements does the same for financing by the banking sector. There are also databases that capture information on market-based sources of financing collated by private companies such as Dealogic. Annex 3A provides a summary of the focus and coverage of the key debt databases.

Asymmetries in debt data also stem from a whole range of factors, including differences in coverage, timing of recording, institutional practice, and delayed reporting by borrowers and creditors. Coverage often differs—debtor-based systems may exclude private nonguaranteed borrowing, whereas creditor-side data likely capture these flows more comprehensively. Recording practices vary: some compilers adopt accrual-based accounting (recognizing transactions when obligations arise), whereas others use the cash basis method (recording payments when they are made). These divergent practices lead to timing and value mismatches. Another common source of asymmetry is valuation, which uses different exchange rates or accounting methods.

For example, compilations based on the face value versus the market value for bond issues will result in very different figures for outstanding balances. Divergent valuation rules for inflation-indexed or floating-rate instruments can further widen the gap between data sets.

Numerous inconsistencies also occur in instrument classification and sectorization—that is, how borrowers are classified and captured in public or private sector debt data. Methodological discrepancies are frequently embedded in national statistical practices and international reporting frameworks, creating challenges for users trying to reconcile external and public debt data across sources. Trade credits and advances may be included in external debt statistics in some countries and unaccounted for in others. Loans extended by state-owned banks may be classified as public debt on the creditor side but recorded as private debt by the debtor.

Differences in the classification of borrowers, particularly SOEs, central banks, and government-guaranteed entities, can lead to significant discrepancies between data sets. Some statistical systems treat SOEs as part of the public sector, whereas others classify them as private unless explicitly guaranteed. Similarly, contingent liabilities and guarantees may be included in debt totals in some frameworks but excluded until they are triggered in others, producing further divergence in reported figures.

International institutions have stepped up efforts to harmonize the compilation of debt statistics. The IMF and the Task Force on Finance Statistics promote the use of standardized statistical frameworks such as External Debt Statistics: Guide for Compilers and Users (IMF 2014) and are currently supporting updates to better account for evolving borrowing trends, including state-contingent debt instruments and collateralized borrowing. The Quarterly External Debt Statistics platform, comanaged by the IMF and the World Bank Group, enables countries to submit quarterly data aligned with international standards, thereby improving consistency and transparency.

metadata.section: From Granular Data to Actionable Knowledge

text: Other important initiatives include the World Bank Group Debt Transparency Initiatives and the IDA Sustainable Development Finance Policy, both of which tie financial support to improvements in debt reporting.

metadata.section: From Granular Data to Actionable Knowledge

text: As already discussed, the core objective of the major revamp of the World Bank Group DRS is harmonization of reporting standards and definitions for LMICs with agreed international methodology, including the IMF’s Integrated Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (IMF 2025) and the United Nations Statistics Division’s 2025 System of National Accounts, supported by dedicated capacity building. Many asymmetries could also be avoided through automation and system integration. Developing centralized platforms that link balance of payments, international investment position statistics, and external debt data, and enable interoperability between debt management systems and other external sector statistics databases, would force consistency and minimize manual errors.

metadata.section: From Granular Data to Actionable Knowledge

text:
Emerging technologies such as discrepancy detectors powered by artificial intelligence or SDMX-based data exchanges would further modernize data compilation workflows.

From Granular Data to Actionable Knowledge
For more than seven decades, the World Bank Group DRS has transformed detailed information reported by borrowing countries into one of the world’s most comprehensive sources of internationally comparable external debt statistics. It provides a statistical infrastructure for understanding not simply how much countries owe but who borrowed from whom, through which instruments, and on what terms, and how those obligations evolve over time.

metadata.section: From Granular Data to Actionable Knowledge

text: At its core, the program is a continuous data-to-knowledge process. Detailed information reported by borrowing countries is systematically validated, reconciled, and standardized before being transformed into internationally comparable debt statistics. These statistics are then analyzed and placed in their broader economic and financial context, turning granular country reporting

metadata.section: From Granular Data to Actionable Knowledge

text:
into evidence that can inform debt management, debt sustainability assessments, financing decisions, and the global policy debate.

The World Bank Group debt transparency work is built as a continuous chain of value through three-tier architecture (refer to annex 3B for more information on the World Bank Group Debt Statistics three-tier architecture): DRS provides the granular evidence, IDS transforms that evidence into trusted and transparent statistical facts, and the International Debt Report (IDR) converts those facts into analysis and actionable knowledge. Together, these three tiers connect country-level debt reporting to the broader development and policy agenda.

metadata.section: From Granular Data to Actionable Knowledge

text: A loan reported by a national debt office can serve as a globally comparable indicator, reveal a change in creditor or financing patterns, expose an information gap or emerging vulnerability, inform a debt sustainability assessment or restructuring discussion, and contribute to international policy discussions on sustainable finance and debt transparency.

metadata.section: From Granular Data to Actionable Knowledge

text: This process also works in reverse. Transparency gaps, new financing instruments, emerging vulnerabilities, and methodological challenges identified through IDS and IDR analysis feed directly back into the DRS. They inform improvements in reporting requirements, classifications, validation rules, reconciliation procedures, methodological guidance, and engagement with both borrowers and creditors. Debt transparency is therefore not a one-time disclosure exercise but a continuous cycle of reporting, validation, reconciliation, dissemination, analysis, and improvement.

metadata.section: From Granular Data to Actionable Knowledge

text: This architecture is also central to the World Bank Group’s broader debt transparency agenda. Greater transparency about the amount, composition, terms, and creditors of public debt is essential for sound debt management, credible debt sustainability assessments, effective restructuring, and informed lending and investment decisions. By strengthening reporting standards, improving data quality, reconciling debtor and creditor records, expanding the information available to users, and identifying remaining data gaps, the DRS provides the statistical foundation on which greater debt transparency can be built.

metadata.section: From Granular Data to Actionable Knowledge

text: This approach also reflects an important evolution in the international debt transparency agenda: responsibility does not rest solely with borrowing countries. Comprehensive debt transparency requires coordinated action by borrowers, bilateral and multilateral creditors, private lenders, international financial institutions, and other stakeholders. The World Bank Group’s role is increasingly to connect these actors around common definitions, stronger reporting practices, better reconciliation, and more accessible and reliable debt information.

metadata.section: From Granular Data to Actionable Knowledge

text: The result is more than a debt database. It is a global statistical infrastructure for debt transparency that connects individual debt obligations to a broader understanding of financing flows, creditor relationships, fiscal pressures, and debt sustainability, while helping make sovereign borrowing increasingly visible, comparable, credible, and accountable.

Ultimately, strengthening debt transparency comes down to ensuring that public borrowing remains a tool for development rather than a source of vulnerability. By improving the availability and reliability of debt data, countries are better equipped to manage risks, design effective policies, and engage transparently with stakeholders. For creditors and markets, enhanced transparency supports more accurate risk assessment and more efficient allocation of capital. For the international community, it contributes to a more stable and resilient global financial system. Sustained investment in this agenda is not only advisable, but it is also necessary for positive long-term development outcomes.

Annex 3A. Sources of Debt Statistics
Debt statistics originate from a diverse set of sources, classified broadly into debtor-based and creditor-based data sets. Each has unique strengths as well as limitations that may lead to discrepancies.

Debtor-Based Sources
Debtor-based data are sourced from countries that borrow, typically through institutions such as finance ministries, debt management offices, or central banks. These data are reported to international sources like the World Bank Group’s DRS and the IMF’s Balance of Payments and International Investment Position. Although rich in detail, debtor-based data sources reflect the borrower’s operational realities and often omit or underreport certain types of debt, such as short-term borrowing and borrowing in the form of debt securities and private sector liabilities, or debt from SOEs without sovereign guarantees.

The DRS covers long-term public and publicly guaranteed external debt, along with aggregate information for private nonguaranteed debt when available. Data are reported on an instrument-by-instrument basis, providing detailed information on terms, disbursements, debt service, and outstanding amounts. The key strength of the DRS is the depth and consistency of coverage for LMICs, enabling granular analysis. Its main limitation is the absence of short-term debt and certain debt instruments, such as pension fund liabilities (owed to national households but held by nonresidents), currency and deposits, and trade credit and advances. Moreover, the aggregation of private nonguaranteed debt reporting
may mask incomplete coverage and can obscure the characteristics of specific instruments.

The IMF’s Balance of Payments and International Investment Position
frameworks capture external debt as part of the broader international accounts, including components such as direct investment debt, portfolio debt, and other investment debt (for example, loans and trade credit and advances). The key strength of these data is their alignment with global macroeconomic accounts, ensuring comparability across countries. The principal limitation is that they are published in aggregate form, masking important details such as the instrument type, currency composition, interest rate structure, maturity profile, creditor sector, and other specifics like collateralization, governing law, and repayment schedules.

It warrants mention that the use of original maturity in the International Investment Position, and thus the unavailability of statistics on a remaining maturity basis, significantly limits the use of International Investment Position external debt–related statistics for debt sustainability analysis. National debt management systems such as the Commonwealth Secretariat’s Meridian, UNCTAD’s Debt Management and Financial Analysis System, and country-specific custom-built platforms are used by borrowers to record, monitor, and manage public debt, often serving as the source of data submitted to the World Bank Group or IMF. Their strength lies in the operational detail they capture to support day-to-day debt management decisions.

Their limitation lies in inconsistency in how these systems are used and the accuracy and completeness of the data recorded in them. These strengths and limitations vary significantly and largely mirror a country’s institutional and technical capacity.

Creditor-Based Sources
The creditor-based sources reflect the viewpoint of the lending institutions, such as donor governments, commercial banks, and bondholders. These sources include the OECD’s Creditor Reporting System, the Bank for International Settlements statistics, and data collated by the Paris Club. Although these sources often provide visibility into bilateral and private sector lending, their coverage may be limited geographically or in terms of the types of instruments covered. Discrepancies between these sources are at the heart of many data asymmetries. These sources reflect the view of those who provide financing, often more complete for bilateral and private sector debt.

The OECD Creditor Reporting System tracks official bilateral loans and grants from members of the Development Assistance Committee and from export credit agencies. It contains detailed information on aspects such as concessionality, maturity, and the intended purpose of financing. Its key strength is its dedicated

focus on development finance, providing detailed insights into aid flows and related terms. Its main limitation is its restricted coverage to official and officially supported lending by OECD member countries.

text: The Bank for International Settlements compiles data from commercial banks on cross-border claims and liabilities through two primary data sets: Locational Banking Statistics, which reports according to the location of the reporting bank; and Consolidated Banking Statistics, which reports banks’ global claims on other countries. Its strength lies in providing timely data on private financial flows, particularly from the banking sector, making it valuable for near-real-time monitoring of cross-border lending trends. Its limitation is that the data are not at the loan level and may not align with debtor country classifications, reducing its utility for detailed debt instrument analysis or reconciliation with national statistics.

metadata.section: Annex 3B. The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Three-Tier Architecture

text: The Paris Club, private sector data collection entities like Dealogic, and some export credit agencies supply information on bilateral debt restructurings, syndicated loans and international bond issues, and direct and guaranteed export credits. Their strength is that they offer unique insights into certain types of financing—such as officially supported export credits and market-based lending— that are often underrepresented in other data sets. Their limitation is that the information is fragmented, not systematically compiled, and often not publicly available in a timely manner, creating gaps in comprehensive debt monitoring. Annex 3B.

metadata.section: Annex 3B. The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Three-Tier Architecture

text: The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Three-Tier Architecture The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Program operates through a three-tier architecture that progressively transforms granular country reporting into internationally comparable statistics and policy-relevant knowledge, while strengthening transparency at every stage of the process (figure 3B.1). Tier 1: DRS—The Granular Data Foundation Established in 1951, the DRS is one of the world’s longest-running sovereign debt reporting systems. Today, it covers roughly 120 low- and middle-income reporting economies and provides a uniquely detailed historical record extending over more than 70 years.

metadata.section: Annex 3B. The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Three-Tier Architecture

text: IBRD and IDA borrowers report detailed information on their long-term public and publicly guaranteed external debt, including new commitments, outstanding stocks, and annual transactions. Private nonguaranteed external debt is also incorporated in aggregate form. At this first tier, the data answer four fundamental questions: Who borrowed? From whom? On what terms? And what happened to the debt over time? These questions are

text: central to debt transparency, particularly as sovereign financing becomes more complex. LMICs increasingly combine traditional bilateral and multilateral loans with syndicated lending, international bonds, collateralized financing, debt swaps, buybacks, and more sophisticated restructuring operations.

metadata.section: Annex 3B. The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Three-Tier Architecture

text: The DRS provides the granular data infrastructure needed to identify, measure, and track debt exposures over time. At the individual debt level, it captures detailed information on borrowers, creditors, instruments, currencies, commitments, disbursements, debt service, arrears, and restructurings, providing insight not only into the amount of debt outstanding but also into its composition, financing terms, repayment profile, and evolution. As sovereign financing instruments and practices continue to evolve, DRS reporting requirements, classifications, and methodological guidance are continuously strengthened to ensure that this growing complexity is reflected in comprehensive, consistent, and increasingly complete coverage of countries’ debt obligations and financing arrangements.

metadata.section: Annex 3B. The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Three-Tier Architecture

text: Tier 2: IDS—From Granular Records to Trusted and Transparent Statistics Debt transparency depends not only on the availability of information but also on its quality, consistency, comparability, and credibility. Individual debt records become meaningful global statistics only after they have been standardized and made comparable across countries and over time. This transformation takes place through the production of the IDS database.

metadata.section: Annex 3B. The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Three-Tier Architecture

text: The statistical production process involves the compilation of the external debt statistics using standardized methodologies, definitions, and classifications. This process is critical to ensure that published statistics accurately reflect countries’ debt. IDS adds value across four critical dimensions: (a) comparability, through common concepts and classifications across economies; (b) consistency, through reconciliation of stocks, flows, transactions, and revisions; (c) historical series, which make it possible to identify structural changes in global financing; and (d) accessibility, through public databases, downloadable data sets, country and regional tables, and analytical products.

text:
Tier 3: IDR—From Trusted Statistics to Actionable Knowledge
The annual IDR represents the analytical tier of architecture. It combines the depth of the underlying DRS information and the consistency of IDS statistics with economic and policy analysis.

metadata.section: Annex 3B. The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Three-Tier Architecture

text: Where the DRS captures what countries report, and IDS establishes what happened, the IDR examines why it happened, why it matters, who is most exposed and more vulnerable, and what policy makers should watch next. For more than five decades, the World Bank Group’s annual debt publication has documented major transformations in international development finance, from the debt crises of the 1980s and the emergence of global bond markets, to debt-relief initiatives, the rise of new bilateral and private creditors, increasingly complex financing instruments, and today’s environment of elevated borrowing costs and debt service pressures. The IDR places these developments in their wider economic context.

metadata.section: Annex 3B. The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Three-Tier Architecture

text: It serves as both an analytical publication and an important instrument of the World Bank Group’s debt transparency agenda by highlighting where improvements in reporting, disclosure, creditor information, and debt management practices are most needed.
